Dust, CO and [C i]: Cross-calibration of molecular gas mass tracers in metal-rich galaxies across cosmic time

2022Dust, CO and [C i]: Cross-calibration of molecular gas mass tracers in metal-rich galaxies across cosmic time–I
L. Dunne    S. J. Maddox    P. P. Papadopoulos    R. J. Ivison Affiliation: School of Physics & Astronomy, Cardiff University, Queens Buildings, The Parade, Cardiff CF24 3AA Affiliation: Dept of Physics, Section of Astrophysics, Astronomy and Mechanics, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, GR-54124, Greece Affiliation: European Southern Observatory, Karl-Schwarzschild-Strasse 2, D-85748 Garching, Germany    H. L. Gomez ††thanks: E-mail:GomezH@cardiff.ac.uk Affiliation: School of Physics & Astronomy, Cardiff University, Queens Buildings, The Parade, Cardiff CF24 3AA Affiliation: Research Center for Astronomy, Academy of Athens, Soranou Efesiou 4, GR-11527 Athens, Greece
Submitted to MNRAS Main Journal, 2022 Xxxxxx; Manuscript ID: MN-22-XXXX-MJ
Abstract

We present a self-consistent cross-calibration of the three main molecular gas mass tracers in galaxies, namely the 12CO(1–0), [C i](P13{}^{3}P_{1}–P03{}^{3}P_{0}) lines, and the submm dust continuum emission, using a sample of 407 galaxies, ranging from local disks to submillimetre-selected galaxies (SMGs) up to z≈6z\approx 6. A Bayesian statistical method is used to produce galaxy-scale universal calibrations of these molecular gas indicators, that hold over 3–4 orders of magnitude in infrared luminosity, LIRL_{\rm IR}. Regarding the dust continuum, we use a mass-weighted dust temperature, TmwT_{\rm mw}, determined using new empirical relations between temperature and luminosity. We find the average L/MmolM_{\rm mol} gas mass conversion factors (including He) to be α850=6.9×1012​W​Hz−1​M⊙−1\mbox{$\alpha_{850}$}=6.9\times 10^{12}\,\rm W\,Hz^{-1}\,M_{\odot}^{-1}, αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}=4.0 M⊙ (k km s-1 pc2)-1 and αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I}=17.0 M⊙ (k km s-1 pc2)-1, based on the assumption that the mean dust properties of the sample (κH\kappa_{\rm H}= gas-to-dust ratio/dust emissivity) will be similar to those of local metal rich galaxies and the Milky Way. The tracer with the least intrinsic scatter is [C i](1–0), while CO(1–0) has the highest. The conversion factors show a weak but significant correlation with LIRL_{\rm IR} which is not apparent when TmwT_{\rm mw} is held constant. Assuming dust properties typical of metal-rich galaxies, we infer a neutral carbon abundance XC​I=[C0/H2]=1.6×10−5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}=\rm[C^{0}/\mbox{H${}_{2}$}]=1.6\times 10^{-5}, similar to that in the Milky Way. We find no evidence for bi-modality of αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} between main-sequence (MS) galaxies and those with extreme star-formation intensity, i.e. ultraluminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs) and SMGs. The means of the three conversion factors are found to be similar between MS galaxies and ULIRGs/SMGs, to within 10–20 per cent. The overarching conclusion of our work is that, for metal-rich galaxies, near-universal average values for αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}, XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} and κH\kappa_{\rm H} are adequate for global molecular gas estimates within the expected uncertainties. The 1σ\sigma scatter in our optimised values for αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}, XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} and κH\kappa_{\rm H} are 0.14, 0.11 and 0.15 dex respectively.

Keywords: 
ISM: dust, extinction; Galaxies: high redshift; Submillimetre: galaxies, ISM; Radio lines: galaxies, ISM

1 Introduction

The cosmic star-formation rate (SFR) density has declined by more than an order of magnitude during the past ≈8\approx 8 Gyr of cosmic history (Lilly et al., 1996; Madau et al., 1996; Madau & Dickinson, 2014). The driver of star formation is the molecular gas supply in galaxies, and indeed the SFR–stellar mass (SFR–M⋆M_{\star}) relationship known as the galaxy main sequence (MS) is purely a by-product of the relationship between SFR and molecular gas (Baker et al., 2022, e.g.), for unperturbed galaxies with significant gas reserves. A major observational goal is to produce a combined census of the molecular gas – the ‘potential for future star formation’ – and the stellar content – the ‘record of past star formation’ – over this period (Keres et al., 2003; Dunne et al., 2003; Dunne et al., 2011; Zwaan et al., 2004; Zafar et al., 2013; Walter et al., 2014; Decarli et al., 2016; Saintonge et al., 2017; Driver et al., 2018; Rhee et al., 2018; Decarli et al., 2019; Riechers et al., 2019, e.g.).

The molecular gas fraction of a galaxy is a crucial component in models of galaxy formation (Obreschkow et al., 2009; Popping et al., 2014; Lagos et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2018, e.g.) and thus measurements of H2\rm H_{2} and stellar mass over large representative galaxy samples are key requirements for understanding how galaxies have transformed from clouds of gas residing in dark matter haloes into the regular agglomerations of stars we see in the local Universe. While it is clear that CO(1–0)-luminous gas is the phase linked with star formation (Wong & Blitz, 2002, e.g.), observations of molecules with higher critical densities (e.g. HCN) revealed that it is the dense H2 gas phase (n>104n>10^{4} cm-3) that correlates most tightly and linearly with tracers of star-formation (Gao & Solomon, 2004).

Atomic hydrogen (H i), on the other hand, constitutes a longer-term gas reservoir for star formation, where under certain conditions of pressure, far-UV radiation field, density and metallicity, a phase transition H i →\rightarrow H2 takes place, catalysed by dust grains (Elmegreen, 1993; Papadopoulos et al., 2002; Blitz & Rosolowsky, 2006, e.g.): a picture supported by numerous observations (Honma et al., 1995; Leroy et al., 2008; Bigiel et al., 2008; Schruba et al., 2011, e.g.). This transition occurs in the inner H i distribution of galaxies, in the cold neutral medium (CNM: n∼50n\sim 50–100 cm-3, Tkin∼100T_{\rm kin}\sim 100–200 k), meanwhile pure H i gas often extends many optical radii beyond the luminous stellar disk (Péroux & Howk, 2020, e.g.), where it can be found concomitant with cold dust (e.g. Thomas et al., 2002).

Unlike H i and its hyperfine line emission at 21 cm, the H2 molecule in its S(0):J=2−0J=2-0 transition at 28μ\mum (the least excitation-demanding H2\rm H_{2} line) is essentially invisible at temperatures typical of giant molecular clouds (10–20 k). This is because its Δ​E/kB\Delta E/k_{\rm B}∼\sim510​k510\,{\sc k}, limits its excitation and detetection only to shocked regions of molecular clouds, where gas temperatures can rise past ∼1000\sim 1000 k, for small (∼1\sim 1–2 per cent) gas mass fractions. Even then, to observe this H2 line at 28 μ\mum requires space-borne telescopes.

For these reasons the rotational transitions of CO (the next most abundant molecule with [CO/H2]∼10−4\rm[CO/H_{2}]\sim 10^{-4}) are commonly used to trace H2\rm H_{2} gas, with the lowest transition (12CO J=1J=1–0) being the most established tracer. Its E10/kB∼5.5E_{10}/k_{\rm B}\sim 5.5 k ensures a well-populated upper level even in the coldest gas, while its low critical density, ncr∼400n_{\rm cr}\sim 400 cm-3, ensures its excitation even at low densities11 1 Because the CO(1–0) line is typically optically thick, with τ10∼5\tau_{10}\sim 5–10 (Bryant & Scoville, 1996; Papadopoulos et al., 2012a, e.g.: their Eqn. 11), the effective critical density is lower still: ncr​(β10)=β10​ncrit∼40n_{\rm cr}(\beta_{10})=\beta_{10}n_{\rm crit}\sim 40–80 cm-3, where β10=(1−e−τ10)/τ10\beta_{10}=(1-e^{-\tau_{10}})/\tau_{10} is the line escape probability..

The CO(1–0) line has significant optical depths in the typically macro-turbulent H2\rm H_{2} gas, though these arise locally within the velocity-coherent gas cells allowing the CO emission to trace gas mass throughout molecular clouds (Dickman et al., 1986, e.g.). The conversion factor, αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}, in the relation MH2=αCOLCO′\mbox{$M_{\rm H2}$}=\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$} cannot be determined using standard optically thin line formation physics due to the high line optical depths. This created the need for a αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} calibration as soon as the ubiquity of CO line emission in H2 clouds was established. Observational and theoretical investigation of αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} suggests it is sensitive to metallicity, molecular gas surface density and kinematic state in galaxies (Pelupessy & Papadopoulos, 2009; Narayanan et al., 2011; Papadopoulos et al., 2012a; Bolatto et al., 2013, e.g.).

Three distinct problems are now recognised regarding the use of CO as a global tracer of H2 mass in galaxies:

  1. 1.

    The αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} factor is sensitive – in a highly non-linear fashion – to the ISM metallicity and ambient far-UV radiation fields (Israel, 1997; Pak et al., 1998; Bolatto et al., 2013, e.g.).

  2. 2.

    Non-self-gravitating molecular clouds – and/or very different average ISM states in terms of average temperature and gas density range from those found in spiral galaxies where αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} was first calibrated – can yield systematically different αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} factors. For example, αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}∼1/5−1/4×\sim 1/5-1/4\times Galactic was initially reported for a sample of four ULIRGs by Downes & Solomon (1998).

  3. 3.

    Elevated cosmic ray (CR) energy densities can destroy CO below a certain gas density threshold, leaving behind more C-rich gas. This density threshold depends on the CR energy density in a highly non-linear fashion, as explored by Bisbas et al. (2015), who found that regions of CO suppression may occur even in moderately enhanced CR conditions if the gas density is low, while the very high CR energy densities expected in ultraluminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs) may be partly compensated by higher gas densities in such starbursts. Modelling [C i/CO] ratios as a function of CR, turbulence, gas density and metallicity is an active area of theoretical research (Bisbas et al., 2015; Bisbas et al., 2017; Bisbas et al., 2021; Glover & Clark, 2016; Clark et al., 2019a; Papadopoulos et al., 2018; Gong et al., 2020, e.g.).

In the distant Universe, additional problems arise. High-redshift galaxies are often observed solely in high-JJ CO lines (J=3J=3–2 and higher), due to the observational challenge of observing the two low-JJ CO lines22 2 Prior to the commissioning of its bands 1 and 2, low-JJ lines from high-redshift galaxies are inaccessible to the Atacama Large Millimetre Array (ALMA). The Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA), the Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) and the Greenbank Telescope (GBT), have in some cases been able to access the faint low-JJ (Ju≤2J_{\rm u}\leq 2) CO lines, but it requires huge amounts of observing time in the best available weather.. Using the high-JJ lines means that global CO(J+1,JJ+1,J)/(1–0) ratios must be assumed before an αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} factor can be used; given the wide range of CO spectral-line energy distributions (SLEDs) found for LIRGs for J=3J=3–2 and higher (Papadopoulos et al., 2012b; Greve et al., 2014; Kamenetzky et al., 2016), these assumptions come with large uncertainties. Finally, at the highest redshifts (≳\ga4), low-JJ CO lines (and dust emission) can be severely suppressed for cold gas (and dust) reservoirs due to their low contrast against the ambient, rest-frame cosmic microwave background (da Cunha et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016).

In principle, radiative transfer models of well-sampled CO (and 13CO) SLEDs can yield αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} values appropriate for a particular galaxy (or even galaxy class) (Papadopoulos et al., 2012b; Papadopoulos et al., 2014; Harrington et al., 2021, e.g.). Nevertheless, the size of the CO line datasets per galaxy required to do this make it impractical (in terms of telescope time) to obtain MM(H2) for large galaxy samples. Amassing a large sample typically means only one or two lines can be gathered per galaxy, and thus a calibration of αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} and its uncertainties remains very valuable. The only practical way to achieve this is to cross-calibrate against the other galaxy-scale H2\rm H_{2} mass tracers.

Large-area far-infrared (FIR) and submillimetre (submm) surveys (Armus et al., 2009; Eales et al., 2010; Vieira et al., 2010; Kennicutt et al., 2011; Oliver et al., 2012; Hodge et al., 2013, e.g.) ushered in a new era in which submm continuum emission from dust has been used widely as an alternative tracer of MH2M_{\rm H2}, although it has been clear that submm-derived dust masses (∝L850\propto\mbox{$L_{850}$}) and CO-derived molecular gas masses (∝LCO′\propto\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$}) are tightly correlated ever since the first statistical submm survey of 100 local FIR-bright galaxies (Dunne et al., 2000, SLUGS –). The first suggestions to use dust as an alternative to CO at high redshift (Santini et al., 2010; Magdis et al., 2012; Scoville et al., 2014, e.g.) were followed quickly by work demonstrating its potential (Scoville et al., 2016; Hughes et al., 2017; Orellana et al., 2017, e.g).

An advantage of using submm continuum emission from dust as an H2\rm H_{2} gas tracer is that it becomes easier to measure at high redshift, because of the negative KK-correction (Blain & Longair, 1993, e.g.), while recent technological advances made it possible to image areas large enough to be free of cosmic variance, leading to the FIR/submm detection of many thousands of galaxies by the Herschel Space Observatory, for example. The use of dust as a gas mass proxy requires an estimate of metallicity, since the dust-to-gas ratio, δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}, is roughly proportional to metallicity (Muñoz-Mateos et al., 2009; Magdis et al., 2012; Sandstrom et al., 2013; Draine et al., 2014, e.g.). The appropriate δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR} can then be applied (Valentino et al., 2018, e.g.). Whilst this requirement is often raised as a problem regarding the use of dust as a gas mass tracer, its dependence on metallicity is in fact weaker than that of CO33 3 Moreover, since H2\rm H_{2} cannot be traced (in bulk) by any of its own lines, regardless of which other tracer (X) is used (dust emission, CO, or 13CO, or C i line emission), it will always be necessary to assume a [X/H2]\rm[X/H_{2}] abundance in order to proceed to a final H2\rm H_{2} gas mass estimate..

For galaxies selected at FIR/submm/mm wavelengths, it is safe to assume that the metallicity will be high, such that δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR} will be broadly similar to those found for local metal-rich spirals and the Milky Way (Dunne & Eales, 2001; Draine, 2009; Magdis et al., 2012; Sandstrom et al., 2013; Rowlands et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2017; Berta et al., 2021). A detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of using dust as a tracer of gas can be found in Genzel et al. (2015) and Scoville et al. (2017)44 4 Continuum dust emission does not yield information on kinematics, unlike spectral lines..

A third method of tracing molecular gas – the use of atomic carbon lines – has come to the fore since ALMA became operational. Its promise was recognised by Papadopoulos et al. (2004) and its first application as a tracer for molecular gas mass in galaxies gave good results (Weiß et al., 2003; Papadopoulos & Greve, 2004), implying that: a) the [C i](P13{}^{3}P_{1}–P03{}^{3}P_{0}) lines are optically thin for the bulk of H2\rm H_{2} gas (Pérez-Beaupuits et al., 2015) and b) atomic carbon is present throughout CO-rich molecular cloud volumes.

The latter contradicts the earlier simple plane-parallel PDR model where atomic carbon (and its line emission) occupied only a thin layer, sandwiched between C+\rm C^{+} in the outer and CO in the inner regions of FUV-illuminated molecular clouds (Tielens & Hollenbach, 1985). However observations have repeatedly shown excellent concomitance of C i line emission with CO line emission, by area and by velocity, and C i shows a tighter correlation with 13CO than with 12CO. C i is now thought to arise from same volume as the CO, with similar excitation conditions (Plume et al., 1999; Ikeda et al., 2002; Schneider et al., 2003; Beuther et al., 2014; Pérez-Beaupuits et al., 2015, e.g.). Moreover, it may be that C i lines can also trace CO-dark molecular gas, should such phase exist in galaxies in significant amounts, e.g. due to CR-induced dissociation of CO to C (and O) (Bisbas et al., 2015).

Despite being much fainter than the C+\rm C^{+} line at 158 μ\mum (the prime ISM cooling line), atomic carbon lines do hold certain advantages, namely: a) they solely trace H2\rm H_{2} gas, whereas the C+\rm C^{+} line also traces the H i and H ii gas reservoirs, which can be significant, especially in metal-poor systems (Madden et al., 1997; Liszt, 2011; Papadopoulos & Geach, 2012; Pérez-Beaupuits et al., 2015; Clark et al., 2019a, e.g.); b) the C i lines can remain excited for cold gas (e.g. for [C i](1–0): E10/kB∼24E_{10}/k_{\rm B}\sim 24 k) unlike the C+\rm C^{+} line, where the Δ​E/kB∼92\Delta E/k_{\rm B}\sim 92 k will keep it very faint for cold gas; c) the frequencies of the two C i lines, at 492 and 809 GHz, remain accessible for galaxies over a much larger redshift range (and thus cosmic volume) than the C+\rm C^{+} line. In the latter case, its rest-frame frequency, ν⁡(C+)∼1.9\rm\nu(C^{+})\sim 1.9 THz, means the C+\rm C^{+} line is observable by ALMA’s most sensitive receivers only at z≳4z\ga 4.

Nevertheless, the high rest-frame frequencies of the C i line made early observations (and thus any calibration efforts) in the local Universe very difficult. Initially there had been relatively little observational work outside of the Milky Way, largely confined to extreme systems such as quasars and starburst nuclei (White et al., 1994; Weiß et al., 2005; Walter et al., 2011, e.g.). These studies advocated a higher carbon abundance for these extreme systems, XC​I=[C0/H2]=5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}=\rm[C^{0}/H_{2}]=5–12×10−512\times 10^{-5}, compared to the XC​I=1\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}=1–2.5×10−52.5\times 10^{-5} seen in the Milky Way (Frerking et al., 1989).

More recently, Herschel observed many local galaxies in C i, although the [C i](1–0) line was at the edge of the observable range for the Herschel Fourier Transform Spectrometer (FTS), such that the sensitivity was somewhat compromised. As a result, most of the detected galaxies were either ULIRGs, starbursts or low-metallicity dwarfs (Kamenetzky et al., 2014; Rosenberg et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2017; Jiao et al., 2017). A small sample of normal disk galaxies was mapped in C i (Jiao et al., 2019, hereafter J19 – see also Crocker et al., 2019). J19 studied the spatial distribution of LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} and LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} at a ∼1\sim 1-kpc scale in 15 local galaxies. They concluded that C i is a good tracer of molecular gas, in the sense that it correlates well with CO and the ratio LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} is distributed smoothly across galaxies. Comparing against CO(1–0) maps and the independent estimates of αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} from Sandstrom et al. (2013), these resolved studies suggested XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}=1.3–2.5×10−5\times 10^{-5}, similar to the range in the Galaxy, and that found by the absorber study of Heintz & Watson (2020).

With ALMA now in routine operations, studies of C i have expanded to a broader range of galaxies, with a greater variety of average ISM conditions, over a wider range of redshift. These include SMGs, which lie mainly at z>1z>1 (Alaghband-Zadeh et al., 2013; Bothwell et al., 2017; Popping et al., 2017; Oteo et al., 2018; Nesvadba et al., 2019; Dannerbauer et al., 2019; Gómez-Guijarro et al., 2019, e.g.), and main-sequence (MS) galaxies at z=0.35z=0.35–1.2 (Valentino et al., 2018; Bourne et al., 2019; Valentino et al., 2020; Dunne et al., 2021). C i has even been detected in the intracluster medium of the Spiderweb galaxy cluster at z=2.16z=2.16, as well as in several of its individual galaxies (Emonts et al., 2018). Routine use of C i as a tracer of molecular gas is currently limited by the lack of calibration studies to explore and determine the values and behaviour of the parameters involved, i.e. XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} and αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I}. XC​I=3×10−5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}=3\times 10^{-5} has been adopted by almost all recent studies, taken from Weiß et al. (2003), determined from a comparison of analyses of CO and C i in the centre of M 82, which has unusually high [C0/CO]∼0.5\rm[C^{0}/CO]\sim 0.5, whereas attempts to estimate XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} in other ways – e.g. from absorption studies of Gamma-ray bursts and quasar absorbers (Heintz & Watson, 2020) – have found lower values, consistent with the range seen in the Milky Way.

This paper presents the first dedicated cross-calibration study of the dust, 12CO(1–0) and [C i](P13{}^{3}P_{1}–P03{}^{3}P_{0}) emission in a sample of 407 galaxies from the literature, including MS galaxies and SMGs, such that we can compare their properties and tracer-(H2\rm H_{2} mass) conversion factors. We include the 250-μ\mum-selected galaxies at z=0.35z=0.35 observed with ALMA in all three tracers by Dunne et al. (2021) where our method was first briefly presented.

In §2 we describe the samples used in this analysis, the observables, and the derived quantities. In §3 we describe the Bayesian approach for producing optimised, self-consistent tracer-(H2\rm H_{2}-mass) conversion parameters between multiple tracers simultaneously. We then examine correlations of the observables to look for trends in §4. In §5 we investigate the trends we have found in the conversion factors and provide refined calibration recipes. Finally, in §6 we discuss the results and highlight the open questions. Throughout, we use a cosmology with Ωm=0.27,ΩΛ=0.73\Omega_{\rm m}=0.27,\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.73 and H0=71H_{0}=71 km s-1 Mpc-1.

2 Deriving observational quantities

2.1 Sample

The samples used in our study are those available in the literature – up-to-date as of early 2022 – which have at least two of the three tracers: submm dust continuum emission at λrest>500\lambda_{\rm rest}>500μ\mum, 12CO(1–0) or (2–1), and [C i](P13{}^{3}P_{1}–P03{}^{3}P_{0}). Summarising: 326 galaxies have both CO and submm continuum detections; 140 have both C i and submm dust continuum detections; 109 have both C i and CO detections; 101 have all three tracers. The sample covers the redshift range 0<z<60<z<6, and includes galaxies lying within 1 dex of the MS as well as extreme starbursts such as local ULIRGs and most high-zz submm-selected galaxies. Full details and references are listed in Table 1. Lensed galaxies are included only where there is an estimate of the magnification, μ\mu, and all luminosities have been corrected by the magnification factor. Our sample includes the galaxies from one of the most comprehensive studies of dust as a tracer of molecular gas across cosmic time - Scoville et al. (2016), henceforth Sco1655 5 Although lensed galaxies were included in their work, the luminosities were not de-magnified.. The Scoville et al. sample has been updated as described in Appendix A.

In order to test for the effect of SF intensity or ‘SF-mode’ on any later results, we divide the sample into two groups, referred to hereafter as ‘MS galaxies’ and ‘SMGs’, the names of the groups are not meant to be accurate definitions but rather a reference to familiar categories. For this heterogeneous data-set, defining a simple criterion for two groups is not possible, and even if it were, a fuzzy boundary would still remain due to measurement errors and the inability to capture the complexity in a single parameter. The extreme starburst ‘SMG’ group contains the high-redshift submillimeter selected galaxies which were discovered in the pre-ALMA era and as such are extreme star forming systems (else they could not have been detected), plus the local ULIRGs and some LIRGs which have evidence for very intense and obscured regions (e.g. NGC 4418, IC 860) where conditions are likely to be extreme (Díaz-Santos et al., 2017; Falstad et al., 2021). The ‘MS galaxy’ group contains the lower luminosity local disk galaxies plus the LIRGS which are not extreme, the intermediate redshift sources selected at 250μ\mum from the Herschel-ATLAS – z=0.35z=0.35 galaxies from Dunne et al. (2021) and the z<0.3z<0.3 VALES galaxies (Hughes et al., 2017), the z∼1z\sim 1 galaxies (Valentino et al., 2018; Bourne et al., 2019) and the ASPECs sources denoted as ‘MS’ in that survey (Boogaard et al., 2020). (Full references are provided in Table 1.)

There are two situations where corrections to luminosities may be required:

H i-dominated galaxies at low LIR{}_{\textbf{IR}}.

For galaxies with a large fraction of H i within their optical disk, their dust tracing H i rather than H2 makes a significant contribution to the submm continuum emission. Since our intention is to provide a calibration for H2 rather than total gas, we apply a correction to L850L_{850} for galaxies with fH​I=H i/H2>1\mbox{$f_{\rm H\,I}$}=\mbox{H\,{\sc i}}/\mbox{H${}_{2}$}>1, as described in Appendix B.1. Galaxies corrected in this way are shown as cyan diamonds in the plots.

Local galaxies mapped in C i by the Herschel FTS.

The local galaxies mapped using the Herschel FTS by J19 present some complex issues. Some do not have C i and dust continuum measurements in matched apertures, and those same galaxies are often only detected in C i in the inner few kpc of the galaxy, where the ratios of LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} may also be biased – for example, by a lower αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} in galaxy centres. We discuss the issues in more detail in §4.4 and Appendix B.2. Galaxies requiring a significant correction (>0.1>0.1 dex) to LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} are labelled as C icor; they are shown in the plots as pink diamonds, but not included in the analysis unless specified.

2.2 Observables

We will compare three tracers of molecular gas, where the observables (the luminosities L850L_{850}, LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} and LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}) are empirically related to the molecular gas mass as

Mmol=L850/α850=αCOLCO′=αC​ILC​I′\mbox{$M_{\rm mol}$}=\mbox{$L_{850}$}/\mbox{$\alpha_{850}$}=\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$}=\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}$} (1)

The goal of this analysis is to determine self-consistent conversion factors α850\alpha_{850}, αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} and αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} and study the physical properties they depend on, e.g. C abundance, gas-to-dust ratio (δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}), dust emissivity. Our definition of the ‘observables’ is intended to be independent of as many assumptions as possible. For CO and C i, we use L′L^{\prime} as defined by Solomon & Vanden Bout (2005):

L′=3.25×107νrest2​(DL21+z)​[∫Δ​VS​𝑑vJy​km​s−1]​K​km​s−1​pc2,L^{\prime}=\frac{3.25\times 10^{7}}{\nu_{\rm rest}^{2}}\left(\frac{D_{\rm L}^{2}}{1+z}\right)\left[\frac{\int_{\Delta V}Sdv}{\rm Jy\,km\,s^{-1}}\right]\,\,\,\,{\rm K\,km\,s}^{-1}\,{\rm pc}^{2}, (2)

where ∫Δ​VS​𝑑v\int_{\Delta V}Sdv is the velocity-integrated line flux density, DLD_{\rm L} is the luminosity distance (Mpc), and νrest\nu_{\rm rest} is the rest frequency66 6 Where we use νrest\nu_{\rm rest}, Solomon & Vanden Bout (2005) use νobs\nu_{\rm obs}, hence the different exponent for (1+z)(1+z) cf. their equation (3). of the transition in GHz.

Most of the galaxies in our compilation have been observed in the 12CO(J=1J=1–0) transition. However, some observations at high redshift target the 12CO(J=2J=2–1) line. We convert L21′L^{\prime}_{21} to L10′L^{\prime}_{10} using the line luminosity ratio R21=0.8R_{21}=0.8; if instead we were to set R21R_{21} to unity, this would not affect any of our conclusions. We do not use J≥3J\geq 3 CO lines because the uncertainties in the global excitation corrections become too large for a useful calibration study.

We use only the C i P13{}^{3}P_{1}–P03{}^{3}P_{0} line, as it is the least sensitive to the average excitation conditions, and correlates better with the low-JJ CO emission (Jiao et al., 2017; Jiao et al., 2019; Crocker et al., 2019). Moreover, there is now evidence of strongly sub-thermal excitation for C i(2–1) (Harrington et al., 2021; Papadopoulos et al., 2022), making it difficult to use this line as an H2\rm H_{2} mass tracer since its excitation is extremely uncertain.

For the dust continuum emission, we use L850L_{850}, the luminosity at rest-frame 850 μ\mum:

L850=4​π​Sν⁡(obs)×K⁡(DL21+z)​W​Hz−1,\mbox{$L_{850}$}=4\pi S_{\rm{\nu(obs)}}\times K\left(\frac{D_{\rm L}^{2}}{1+z}\right)\,\,\,\,\,{\rm W\,Hz}^{-1}, (3)

where DLD_{\rm L} is the luminosity distance, Sν⁡(obs)S_{\rm{\nu(obs)}} is the observed flux density and KK is the KK-correction to rest-frame 850μ\mum, defined as

K=(353​GHzνrest)3+β​(eh​νrest/k​Td−1e16.956/Td−1).K=\left(\rm{\frac{353\,GHz}{\nu_{\rm rest}}}\right)^{3+\beta}\,\left(\frac{e^{\rm{h\nu_{\rm rest}/k\mbox{$T_{\rm d}$}}}-1}{e^{16.956/\mbox{$T_{\rm d}$}}-1}\right). (4)

Here, νrest=νobs​(1+z)\nu_{\rm rest}=\nu_{\rm obs}(1+z), TdT_{\rm d} is the luminosity-weighted dust temperature, from an isothermal fit to the spectral energy distribution (SED) with the dust emissivity, β\beta, allowed to vary between 1.8–2.0.

Sco16 assumed a TdT_{\rm d}=25 k and β=1.8\beta=1.8, respectively, to extrapolate (or KK correct) their observed submm luminosities to rest-frame 850 μ\mum. We make full use of the available data to refine this procedure as follows: 1) With sufficient data, we fit the SED ourselves with β=1.8\beta=1.8 and estimate the rest-frame 850 μ\mum luminosity directly from the SED fit. 2) Failing that, we use the reported TdT_{\rm d} in the literature to make the extrapolation from the longest wavelength measurement available. 3) For SMGs with insufficient data points to have had their SED fitted, we adopt their observed average, TdT_{\rm d}=38 k (da Cunha et al., 2015). The bulk of the high-zz samples now have observations between 2-3 mm with ALMA, as such the extrapolation to rest-frame 850μ\mum is small, even at the highest redshifts. The shortest rest-frame wavelengths we deal with are λr∼250\lambda_{r}\sim 250μ\mum for sources at z∼2−3z\sim 2-3 observed at 850μ\mum, which require K-corrections in the range 50–140. However, the important consideration is the potential uncertainty in that K-correction, not its absolute value. We tried alternatively using the Sco16 method of assuming TdT_{\rm d}=25 K to extrapolate to rest-frame L850L_{850} and found a maximum difference of a factor 1.6, with the average being 1.15 times. The true uncertainty due to the SED sampling and K-correction will be smaller than this, as we know from our work in Section 2.3.1 and Figure 4 that the dust temperatures in SMG are much higher than 25 K. We thus do not consider the extrapolation to rest-frame 850μ\mum to be a significant source of uncertainty or bias in this analysis.

2.3 Physical dependencies of gas mass tracers

2.3.1 Dust–H2\rm{H_{2}} calibration

Large dust grains (a∼0.1a\sim 0.1μ\mum) in thermal equilibrium with their incident radiation field emit as a modified black body (MBB), where the emission is related to the mass of hydrogen as:

MH2=Lν4​π​B​(ν,Tmw)​κH​(ν).\mbox{$M_{\rm H2}$}=\frac{L_{\nu}}{4\pi B(\nu,\mbox{$T_{\rm mw}$})}\,\,\,\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}(\nu). (5)

The two physical quantities needed to calibrate dust continuum emission as a tracer of gas are therefore TmwT_{\rm mw} and κH\kappa_{\rm H}. Expressing Eqn 5 in astronomical units for λ=850\lambda=850 μ\mum, we can write:

MH2[M⊙]=6.14×10−14​κH[kg​m−2]​L850[W​Hz−1]​(24.5Tmw)−1.4,\frac{\mbox{$M_{\rm H2}$}}{[\mbox{$\rm M_{\odot}$}]}=6.14\times 10^{-14}\frac{\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}}{[\rm{kg\,m^{-2}}]}\frac{\mbox{$L_{850}$}}{[\rm{W\,Hz^{-1}}]}\left(\frac{24.5}{\mbox{$T_{\rm mw}$}}\right)^{-1.4}, (6)

where we have simplified the exponential term in the Planck function as ∼(24.5/Tmw)1.4\sim(24.5/\mbox{$T_{\rm mw}$})^{1.4} for 17<Tmw<3017<\mbox{$T_{\rm mw}$}<30 k.

The mass-weighted dust temperature, TmwT_{\rm mw}, is often lower than the luminosity-weighted dust temperature, TdT_{\rm d}, as derived from an isothermal MBB fit to the dust SED, because warm dust outshines cold dust per unit mass. There is an excellent discussion of this in the Appendix to Sco16 which we will not repeat here (Dunne & Eales, 2001, see also).

To determine TmwT_{\rm mw}, we require a multi-component MBB fit to a well-sampled dust SED (Dunne & Eales, 2001, e.g.), or an SED fit using a model that allows a range of radiation field strengths, leading to a range of dust temperatures (Draine et al., 2007, e.g.). These methods give broadly consistent results. As a rule of thumb, the range of TmwT_{\rm mw} in local star-forming galaxies is 15–25 k (Dunne & Eales, 2001; Draine et al., 2007; Hunt et al., 2015; Dale & Helou, 2002; da Cunha et al., 2008; Bendo et al., 2015; Clark et al., 2015), increasing to 25–30 k in luminous starbursts at higher redshifts (Rowlands et al., 2014; da Cunha et al., 2015).

As the dust (α850\alpha_{850}) factor is only weakly dependent on the assumed temperature at rest-frame 850 μ\mum, Sco16 and others assumed a constant TmwT_{\rm mw}=25 k. If instead the true TmwT_{\rm mw} were to be 15 [30] k, the dust and gas mass would be under-[over-]estimated by a factor ∼2×\sim 2\times [1.3×1.3\times], which is overshadowed by the other uncertainties. On the other hand, failure to account for any systematic trend of TmwT_{\rm mw} with another physical parameter can introduce or mask correlations of the conversion factors with that physical parameter.

We therefore explore the validity of assuming constant TmwT_{\rm mw} by collating measurements of TmwT_{\rm mw} from the literature (Dunne & Eales, 2001; Hunt et al., 2019), and additionally making our own fits where possible. In Fig. 1 we show that there are indeed strong correlations of TmwT_{\rm mw} with the observables, namely zz, LIRL_{\rm IR} and the SED colour, LIRL_{\rm IR}/L850L_{850}. There is a clear difference between samples with low and high SFRs, with ⟨Tmw​(MS)⟩=23.0±0.4\langle\mbox{$T_{\rm mw}$}(\rm MS)\rangle=23.0\pm 0.4 k while ⟨Tmw​(SMG)⟩=30.1±0.7\langle\mbox{$T_{\rm mw}$}(\rm SMG)\rangle=30.1\pm 0.7 k. We fit empirical relations for the correlations in Fig. 1 (see Table 4). Where there is no direct estimate of TmwT_{\rm mw} from an SED fit, which is the case for two-thirds of galaxies, we use these empirical relations77 7 We restrict the predicted TmwT_{\rm mw} such that Tmw≤Td\mbox{$T_{\rm mw}$}\leq\mbox{$T_{\rm d}$}. to derive TmwT_{\rm mw} for use in our subsequent analysis. Appendix H.2 compares our approach, where we use individual estimates of TmwT_{\rm mw}, to the adoption of a constant TmwT_{\rm mw}=25 k, where we will discuss those findings in §5.

In their work on strongly lensed SMGs at high redshift, which includes dust continuum emission as a constraint in a large-velocity gradient (LVG) model, Harrington et al. (2021) find that TdT_{\rm d}∼\sim TmwT_{\rm mw} for most SMGs, with both measures of temperature higher than the TmwT_{\rm mw}=25 k commonly used in the literature. To ensure consistency with our other estimates of TdT_{\rm d}, we fitted the Harrington et al. (2021) photometry with three simple models: 1) an isothermal optically thin MBB; 2) an MBB with variable optical depth and – where there were enough data – 3) a two-component MBB. In agreement with Harrington et al., we find that a single dust temperature adequately describes the SED of these galaxies, in contrast to lower redshift (U)LIRGs and normal galaxies which are better fit with multiple dust components (TdT_{\rm d} >> TmwT_{\rm mw}) and/or fits with higher FIR optical depths. The temperatures from the Harrington et al. turbulence model correlate best with our isothermal TdT_{\rm d} meansurements for these galaxies, and the temperatures returned when allowing variable optical depth, Td​(τ)\mbox{$T_{\rm d}$}(\tau), are always significantly higher than those from the Harrington et al. model. We therefore do not use optically thick fits to yield TmwT_{\rm mw} for our high-redshift SMGs. We instead use two-component SED fits to the lensed Planck sources and the handful of SMGs with sufficient data for the empirical relations shown in Fig. 5.

The other key physical parameter in the dust–H2 conversion is κH\kappa_{\rm H}, which is a combination of the dust mass absorption coefficient (κ850\kappa_{850}) and δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}, such that88 8 Literature studies generally present the dust-H2 conversion in terms of δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR} for a fixed emissivity, κ850\kappa_{850}. Given the mounting evidence that κ850\kappa_{850} varies within our own (Remy et al., 2017; Ysard et al., 2015; Ysard et al., 2018; Köhler et al., 2015) and other galaxies (e.g. Clark et al., 2019b, but see also Priestley & Whitworth 2020), we prefer to work with κH\kappa_{\rm H} to avoid projecting all the variation in the H2\rm H_{2}-dust conversion factor onto δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}. κH\kappa_{\rm H}= δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}/κ850\kappa_{850}. Briefly, κ850\kappa_{850} is sensitive to the grain composition and structure (amorphous; crystalline; coagulated; mantled), while δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR} is roughly proportional to metallicity and, for galaxies with metallicity within a factor 2 of Z⊙Z_{\odot}, as expected for those in our samples, can be taken to be roughly constant, at δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}=100=100–150 (Sodroski et al., 1997; Dunne et al., 2000; Dunne & Eales, 2001; Draine et al., 2007; Muñoz-Mateos et al., 2009; Leroy et al., 2011; Sandstrom et al., 2013; Planck Collaboration et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2017; De Vis et al., 2021).

Fortunately, observational measures of κH\kappa_{\rm H} are available, both for the Milky Way and for external galaxies, with values of κH\kappa_{\rm H} ∼2000\sim 2000 kg m-2 in the Milky Way’s diffuse interstellar medium (ISM) and κH\kappa_{\rm H} ∼800\sim 800 kg m-2 in dense clouds. Appendix C discusses in more detail how it is measured, and Table 15 provides a comprehensive set of observational and theoretical values for κH\kappa_{\rm H} from the literature.

It is impossible to disentangle the effect of changing dust properties (κ850\kappa_{850}) from changes in δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR} in observational determinations of κH\kappa_{\rm H}. While the decrease in κH\kappa_{\rm H} towards denser sightlines in the Milky Way is thought to be due to the dust grains coagulating in denser environments – a process expected to increase their emissivity (Köhler et al., 2015, e.g.) – there may also be some decrease in δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR} if the gas is accreted into dust mantles or ices (i.e. grain growth). Both effects are to be expected (Jones et al., 2017; Jones, 2018, e.g.) and both act to decrease κH\kappa_{\rm H}. Counter to that, the higher estimates of κH\kappa_{\rm H} in the diffuse atomic phase (lowest NHN_{\rm H} sightlines at high latitudes) in the Milky Way may be due in part to a lower dust emissivity for grains without ice mantles, where only the refractory cores remain, subjected to harsher ultraviolet (UV) irradiation. Additionally, there is likely a metallicity gradient at high latitudes, leading to a higher δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}, further increasing κH\kappa_{\rm H}. There is thus a qualitative expectation that denser regions with higher metallicity will have higher dust emissivity, κ850\kappa_{850}, and lower δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}, producing a lower κH\kappa_{\rm H}. More diffuse regions with lower metallicity will move in the opposite direction. In §5, we find that we can constrain the range of κH\kappa_{\rm H}, at least, and therefore the combination of δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}/κ850\kappa_{850}.

2.3.2 C​I\rm C\,I–H2\rm{H_{2}} calibration

Here, we introduce the two physical parameters the XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}=[C0/H2]\rm[C^{0}/H_{2}] average abundance ratio and the average excitation factor Q10Q_{10}=N1/Ntot=\rm N_{1}/N_{tot}, pertinent to the use of C i as a tracer of H2. The relationship between MH2M_{\rm H2} and the ‘observable’ – [C i](1–0) line emission – is (in astronomical units):

MH2​(M⊙)=0.0127XC​I​Q10​(DL21+z)​[∫Δ​VS[CI]​(1−0)​𝑑vJy​km​s−1]\mbox{$M_{\rm H2}$}({\rm M}_{\odot})=\frac{0.0127}{X_{\rm C\,I}\,\,Q_{10}}\left(\frac{D_{\rm L}^{2}}{1+z}\right)\,\,\left[\frac{\int_{\Delta V}S_{\rm[CI](1-0)}dv}{\rm Jy\,km\,s^{-1}}\right] (7)

with DLD_{\rm L} in Mpc and ∫Δ​VS[CI]​(1−0)​Δ​v\int_{\Delta V}S_{\rm[CI](1-0)}\Delta v in Jy km s-1. Expressed in units of line luminosity, this becomes:

MH2​(M⊙)=9.51×10−5XC​I​Q10​LC​I′.\mbox{$M_{\rm H2}$}(\mbox{$\rm M_{\odot}$})=\frac{9.51\times 10^{-5}}{\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}\,Q_{10}}\,\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}$}. (8)

The excitation term, Q10Q_{10}, describes the relative fraction of carbon atoms in the J=1J=1 state. Under general non-LTE conditions it is a function of both gas density, nn, and TkT_{\rm k}  and is derived analytically in the Appendix to Papadopoulos, Thi & Viti (2004). A recent study of the [C i](2–1)/(1–0) line ratio (Papadopoulos, Dunne & Maddox, 2022) finds that the C i lines are both sub-thermally excited in the ISM of galaxies, with the [C i](2–1) especially so (Harrington et al., 2021, see also). Thus the LTE expressions for Q10Q_{10} should not be used, nor will the C i line ratio produce an estimate of TkT_{\rm k} (both methods having been widely used in the literature to date). Details for Q10Q_{10} are in the Appendix D, but in summary we find:

  1. 1.

    The [C i](1–0) excitation term, Q10Q_{10}, is a non-trivial function of density and temperature, but for the range Tk≥20\mbox{$T_{\rm k}$}\geq 20 K and log n≥2.5n\geq 2.5 – which is where the bulk of H2 in star forming galaxies is thought to reside – ⟨Q10⟩=0.48±0.08\langle\mbox{$Q_{10}$}\rangle=0.48\pm 0.08 where the 99 per cent confidence range is quoted (see Papadopoulos et al. 2022 and Figure 13 for details).

  2. 2.

    Due to a slight super-thermal behaviour, higher density, higher TkT_{\rm k} conditions can produce similar or even lower Q10Q_{10} than lower density, lower TkT_{\rm k} conditions. This breaks any intuitive link between Q10Q_{10} and the ISM conditions, i.e. we do not necessarily expect a higher Q10Q_{10} in SMGs compared to MS galaxies (see Fig. 13).

  3. 3.

    As the [C i](2–1) line is even more strongly sub-thermally excited, its Q21=N2/NtotQ_{21}=N_{2}/N_{\rm tot} factor varies strongly99 9 The Q21​(n,Tk)Q_{21}(n,T_{k}) that enters the estimates of molecular gas mass when the [C i](2–1) line is used can vary almost by a factor of ∼5\sim 5, depending on (n,Tk)(n,T_{k}).. This is the main reason why our current study is restricted to the [C i](1–0) line.

As the [C i](P13{}^{3}P_{1}–P03{}^{3}P_{0}) line is optically thin for most conditions expected in spiral disks (Weiß et al., 2005; Pérez-Beaupuits et al., 2015; Harrington et al., 2021), the relationship between LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} and MH2M_{\rm H2} is proportional to XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} – the abundance of carbon atoms relative to H2. This dependence on abundance is as expected for any method that employs tracers of H2\rm H_{2} gas mass other than the H2\rm H_{2} lines themselves1010 10 Even for optically thick tracers of H2\rm H_{2} gas, such as CO(1–0) line emission, a [CO/H2]\rm[CO/H_{2}] abundance still enters the method via the CO–H2 cloud volume-filling factor, fCOf_{\rm CO}, albeit not in a sensitive fashion unless a combination of strong FUV radiation and/or low metallicities selectively dissociate CO in the outer cloud layers while leaving the largely self-shielding H2\rm H_{2} intact (then fCOf_{\rm CO} can be ≪1\ll 1, see Pak et al. 1998 for details)..

With the excitation factor Q10Q_{10} varying no more than 16 per cent over the typical range of H2 conditions in galaxies (Tk≥20\mbox{$T_{\rm k}$}\geq 20 K, log n≥2.5n\geq 2.5), the major source of uncertainty in C i-based molecular gas mass estimates (and thus the major source of scatter in the αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} conversion factor) is the neutral carbon abundance, XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}. The relatively recent introduction of the [C i](1–0) line as a gas tracer means that XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} has not been widely explored – constraining it and investigating any potential trends is a key outcome of our cross-calibration work.

In the Milky Way, XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} is found to vary only modestly, from 0.8–2.2×10−52.2\times 10^{-5} (Zmuidzinas et al., 1988; Frerking et al., 1989; Tauber et al., 1995; Ikeda et al., 2002, e.g.), while a much higher value (XC​I=5×10−5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}=5\times 10^{-5}) has been inferred for the nearby starburst nucleus of M 82 (Schilke et al., 1993; White et al., 1994; Stutzki et al., 1997)1111 11 The measurement is in fact the [C0/CO]\rm[C^{0}/CO] abundance, and a value for [CO/H2] has then to be assumed to infer XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}.. Thanks to ALMA, very high localised ratios of LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} (translating to high XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}=5-7×10−5\times 10^{-5}) have also been measured in extreme regions, such as the Circum-Nuclear Disk (CND) of NGC 7469 which is believed to host an X-ray Dominated Region (XDR) (Izumi et al., 2020) and the outflow region in NGC 6240 (Cicone et al., 2018). More modestly elevated LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} ratios tend to be found in the central nuclear regions of starburst galaxies (Jiao et al., 2019; Salak et al., 2019; Saito et al., 2020). However, when averaged over larger kpc scale regions – the ratios become consistent with the average global ratios measured for this sample (see Figure 5). Independent measurements of XC​I=1.6−0.7+1.3×10−5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}=1.6^{+1.3}_{-0.7}\times 10^{-5} (for solar metallicity) were made by Heintz & Watson (2020) using UV absorption measures for a range of absorber systems across cosmic time. Cosmic rays (and X-rays) are expected to dissociate CO in favour of atomic carbon, increasing [C0/CO][{\rm C}^{0}/{\rm CO}], a hypothesis supported by both simulations and observations (Bisbas et al., 2015; Clark et al., 2019a; Israel, 2020; Izumi et al., 2020, e.g.).

2.3.3 CO–H2\rm{H_{2}} calibration

The 12CO(1–0) line is optically thick in most (but not all see Aalto et al., 1995, e.g.) ISM conditions expected in galaxies. Unlike dust continuum emission where optical depths build up over large columns of dust, the entire CO line optical depth builds up within very small gas ‘cells’ (<<0.1 pc) due to the very turbulent nature of the velocity fields, and the small thermal line widths (Tauber et al., 1991; Falgarone et al., 1998). This localised nature of CO line optical depths and the macro-turbulent CO line formation mechanism allows a great simplification of the radiative transfer models of such lines, i.e. the use of the so-called Large Velocity Gradient (LVG) approximation. However, it also complicates the relationship between the CO line luminosity and the underlying H2\rm H_{2} gas mass, making the corresponding conversion factor, αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}, dependent on the thermal state of the gas, its average density, as well as its dynamic state.

Following Papadopoulos et al. (2012b) the αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} factor in an LVG setting is given by:

αCO=2.65​nH2Tb​Kvir−1​[M⊙ (k km s-1 pc2)-1]\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=2.65\frac{\sqrt{n_{\rm H2}}}{T_{\rm b}}\,K_{\rm vir}^{-1}\,\,\,\,[\mbox{M${}_{\odot}$\,({\sc k}\,km\,s${}^{-1}$\,pc${}^{2}$)${}^{-1}$}] (9)

where nH2n_{\rm H2} and TbT_{\rm b} are the average density (in cm-3) and the CO(1--0) brightness temperature1212 12 Here the cloud CO-H2 volume filling factor is set fCO=1f_{\rm CO}=1. for the molecular cloud ensemble while KvirK_{\rm vir} describes the average dynamic state of the gas (self-gravitating clouds Kvir∼1K_{\rm vir}\sim 1, unbound clouds Kvir>1K_{\rm vir}>1). In principle, multi-phase LVG models of CO (and 13CO) SLEDs can be used to constrain αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}, but in practice this demands large line datasets per galaxy (Papadopoulos et al., 2014; Harrington et al., 2021, e.g.), making it impractical for use in large galaxy samples. This is why in our study αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} remains an empirical conversion factor to be (cross)-calibrated.

2.3.4 Conversion factors and physical parameters

The two optically thin tracers – thermal dust continuum emission and C i – have a simple relation between the empirical ‘mass-to-light’ conversion parameter (αX\alpha_{\rm X}) and the physical conditions in the ISM (e.g. abundance, emissivity, temperature). We can write the empirical factors (Eqn. 1) in terms of these physical parameters as follows1313 13 Hereafter we omit the units for αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}, αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} and α850\alpha_{850}.:

α850=1.628×10161.36​κH​(24.5Tmw)−1.4​W​Hz−1​Mmol−1,\mbox{$\alpha_{850}$}=\frac{1.628\times 10^{16}}{1.36\,\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}}\left(\frac{24.5}{\mbox{$T_{\rm mw}$}}\right)^{-1.4}\,\,\,{\rm W\,Hz}^{-1}{\rm M}_{\rm mol}^{-1}\,\,, (10)

where the factor 1.36 corrects to total molecular mass, including He.

αC​I=16.8​[XC​I1.6×10−5]−1​[Q100.48]−1​M⊙​(K​km​s−1​pc2)−1\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}=16.8\,\left[\frac{\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}}{1.6\times 10^{-5}}\right]^{-1}\left[\frac{Q_{10}}{0.48}\right]^{-1}\,\,\,\rm{\mbox{$\rm M_{\odot}$}\,(K\,km\,s^{-1}\,pc^{2})^{-1}} (11)

Eqn. 11 also includes the factor 1.36 for He.

3 Deriving self-consistent calibration of conversion factors

We next describe how we combine the measurements of multiple gas tracers in the most efficient way, in order to determine their cross-calibrations. Our goal is to find the empirical conversion factors (α850\alpha_{850}, αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I}, αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}) or physical parameters (κH\kappa_{\rm H}, XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}), which produce a consistent estimate for MH2M_{\rm H2} in a given galaxy.

Our dataset provides nested samples, each with a different set of available gas tracers. The daX sample has all three tracers available – dust continuum, CO and C i, and contains 101 galaxies (NdaXN_{\rm daX} = 101). The names and statistics for the other samples are as follows: ad – CO and dust, NadN_{\rm ad} = 326; Xd – C i and dust, NXdN_{\rm Xd} = 140; Xa – C i and CO, NXaN_{\rm Xa} = 109. The properties of these samples are in Table 2.

The best constraints at log10 LIRL_{\rm IR} >11>111414 14 Hereafter we will refer to log10\log_{10} as simply log. come from the daX sample because it has three independent tracers of gas mass, but it lacks coverage of luminosities below lIR=11l_{\rm IR}=11. The ad sample is the largest and spans the widest range in LIRL_{\rm IR}, reflecting the longer time for which CO observations have been possible for nearby galaxies.

We begin with the daX sample, to illustrate the method of optimisation for the estimates of all three conversion factors simultaneously.1515 15 This method was first presented in brief in Dunne et al. (2021), where it was applied to the sample of z=0.35z=0.35 galaxies. There are four unknowns namely: m=log⁡(MH2)m={\rm log}(\mbox{$M_{\rm H2}$}), X=log⁡(XC​I)X={\rm log}(\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}), κ=log⁡(κH)\kappa={\rm log}(\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}), and α=log⁡(αCO)\alpha={\rm log}(\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}), and three observables: LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}, LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} and L850L_{850}.

With an independent measure of the true MH2M_{\rm H2}, the observables would provide direct estimates of the three conversion factors; however, the value of MH2M_{\rm H2} is not known a priori, so we must use a probabilistic argument based on the fact the observations do provide constraints on the relative values of the conversion factors for each galaxy. There is thus a set of self-consistent conversion factors which link the observables to the true MH2M_{\rm H2}, with an unknown common constant factor.

The Bayesian approach we use is described in detail in Appendix F and requires an estimate of the intrinsic scatter for the logarithms of each of the factors: sXs_{\rm X}, sκs_{\kappa} and sαs_{\alpha}. The observable luminosities relate to these factors as follows, where the coefficients of proportionality are listed in Table 3:

LCO′LC​I′∝αCOXC​I,\displaystyle\frac{\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$}}{\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}$}}\propto\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}, L850LC​I′∝κHXC​I,\displaystyle\frac{\mbox{$L_{850}$}}{\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}$}}\propto\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$},\, LCO′L850∝αCOκH.\displaystyle\frac{\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$}}{\mbox{$L_{850}$}}\propto\frac{\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}}{\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}}. (12)

We begin by measuring the intrinsic scatter between the three pairs of observables using an orthogonal distance regression (ODR) fitting method, which includes the intrinsic scatter, λ\lambda, as a third parameter in the analysis1616 16 We need to multiply λ\lambda from the ODR fitting routine by 2\sqrt{2} because we need to know the intrinsic scatter of X−YX-Y in our dataset in order to determine the intrinsic scatter of each conversion factor in turn. (see Appendix I for full details). The three pair variances derived from the data are then used to estimate the intrinsic variance of the three individual conversion factors (the derivation can be found in Appendix E). The values of the intrinsic scatter for the parameters are given in Table 3, with XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} having the smallest scatter between galaxies. This finding is purely empirical, requiring no assumptions about the values or trends of the conversion factors, and as such is very interesting.

As we do not have any independent measure of the gas mass with which to normalise our cross-calibration (four unknowns but only three measurements), we must make an assumption about the sample average of one of the physical or empirical conversion factors. However, with that assumption made transparent, the individual values can always be scaled to whichever normalisation a reader wishes to adopt. The relative values, however, are always the optimal solution.

We choose to use the dust parameter κH\kappa_{\rm H}= δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}/κ850\kappa_{850} for this normalisation, because there are no trends of L850L_{850}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} or L850L_{850}/LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} with LIRL_{\rm IR} (see Figs 2, 14) and κH\kappa_{\rm H} also has the best observational constraints.

For the Xa sample, where there are no dust continuum measurements, we normalise to XC​IN=1.6×10−5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}^{\rm N}=1.6\times 10^{-5}, which is the mid-range of the values suggested by the independent study of absorption lines by Heintz & Watson (2020).

All the galaxies in our sample are metal rich (0.5<Z/Z⊙<20.5<Z/Z_{\odot}<2) and so we assume that κH\kappa_{\rm H} (δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}) should be similar to that in the Milky Way and other local disks. Throughout the rest of this work, we will use as our reference point the mid-range of extragalactic determinations, κH\kappa_{\rm H}= 1500–2200 kg m-2, which are consistent with measurements of the diffuse ISM in the Milky Way. Our chosen normalisation value, then, is κH\kappa_{\rm H}N = 1884 kg m-2, which is a good match to current theoretical dust models (THEMIS: Jones et al., 2017, and the updated Draine et al., 2007 modified by Hensley & Draine, 2021).

For the standard Milky Way value of δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR} (Jones et al., 2017; Magdis et al., 2012, = 135,), κH\kappa_{\rm H} = 1884 kg m-2 implies that κ850\kappa_{850} = 0.071 m2 kg-1, similar to that used in many extragalactic studies (Dunne et al., 2000; James et al., 2002; da Cunha et al., 2013). For a δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR} fixed to 135, the range of κH\kappa_{\rm H} in extragalactic studies implies a range in κ850\kappa_{850} of 0.06–0.09 m2 kg-1. Table 15 lists κH\kappa_{\rm H} values from extragalactic and Galactic observations, as well as from theoretical dust models.

Note that the choice of normalisation does not affect any of the trends, nor the ratio of the conversion parameters in the pairings; it merely sets the average value of the reference calibration parameter, to which the others are relative.

The sample mean expectation values for the other two parameters, ⟨αCO⟩\langle\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}\rangle and ⟨XC​I⟩\langle\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}\rangle, are next derived from our assumed value of ⟨κH⟩\langle\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}\rangle, together with the mean ratios of the observables listed in Table 3. The effective standard deviation is also calculated – the intrinsic scatter of each parameter added in quadrature to the measurement error for that gas tracer. For example, for CO:

σeff=sα2+σCO2,\sigma_{\rm eff}=\sqrt{s_{\alpha}^{2}+\sigma_{\rm CO}^{2}},

where sαs_{\alpha} is the intrinsic scatter in log(αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}), and σCO\sigma_{\rm CO} is the measurement error on log(LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}).

We can now estimate the probability of finding a particular set of conversion factors for any given galaxy. We use ai,i=1,2,3a_{i},\,i=1,2,3 to denote the logarithms of the three conversion factors1717 17 For ease of representation, a850=−log⁡(α850)a_{850}=-\log(\mbox{$\alpha_{850}$})., and write the mean expectation values and effective standard deviations as ⟨ai⟩\langle a_{i}\rangle, and σi,eff\sigma_{i,\rm eff} respectively. Assuming that these follow Gaussian distributions, the probability of finding the factors, aia_{i}, for any galaxy is:

P∝∏i=1Nexp⁡(−(ai−⟨ai⟩)22​σi,eff2)=exp(−∑i=1N(ai−⟨ai⟩)22​σi,eff2).P\propto\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{N}\exp\left(-\frac{(a_{i}-\langle a_{i}\rangle)^{2}}{2\sigma_{\rm i,eff}^{2}}\right)\\ =\exp\left(-\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{(a_{i}-\langle a_{i}\rangle)^{2}}{2\sigma_{\rm i,eff}^{2}}\right). (13)

Thus, the ratios of observable luminosities for any given galaxy can be used to determine the ratios of conversion factors (Eqn. 12), and the common scaling factor that maximises the probability in Equation 13 is the best estimate of MH2M_{\rm H2}. The derivation in Appendix F shows that this reduces analytically to a simple inverse variance weighted mean, such that:

log⁡MH2opt=∑i=1N(mi×wi)∑i=1Nwi,\log M_{\rm H_{2}}^{\rm opt}=\frac{\sum^{N}_{i=1}(m_{i}\times w_{i})}{\sum^{N}_{i=1}w_{i}}, (14)

where wi=1/σi,eff2w_{i}=1/\sigma_{i,\rm eff}^{2}, and mim_{i} is the log mass estimate for each tracer.

mi=li+⟨ai⟩,m_{i}=l_{i}+\langle a_{i}\rangle,

where lil_{i} is the measured observable (log luminosity) and ⟨ai⟩\langle a_{i}\rangle is the sample mean expectation value for the conversion factor. Once the optimal mass is determined this way, we can then estimate the corresponding optimal conversion factor on a per-galaxy basis, as:

ai=mopt−li.a_{i}=m^{\rm opt}-l_{i}. (15)

The error on the optimal mass is simply the error on the inverse variance weighted mean:

σmopt=(∑i=1Nwi)−1/2,\sigma_{m}^{\rm opt}=\left(\sum^{N}_{i=1}w_{i}\right)^{-1/2}, (16)

and the error on each of the conversion factors, accounting for co-variance is:

σa​i=σmopt2+σl​i2​(1−2​wi∑j=1Nwj),\sigma_{ai}=\sqrt{\sigma_{\rm m^{opt}}^{2}+\sigma_{li}^{2}\left(1-\frac{2w_{i}}{\sum^{N}_{j=1}w_{j}}\right)}, (17)

where σl​i\sigma_{li} is the logarithmic measurement error on the observable quantity, e.g. LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}, LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}, L850L_{850}.

By design, each tracer for a given galaxy, together with its optimised conversion factors, will produce the same gas mass, such that MH2CO=MH2C​I=MH2dust\mbox{$M_{\rm H2}$}^{\rm CO}=\mbox{$M_{\rm H2}$}^{\rm C\,I}=\mbox{$M_{\rm H2}$}^{\rm dust}.

4 Trends in the luminosity ratios

As our cross-calibration process relies on measurements of the luminosity ratios, it is first instructive to look at the trends in these observables to better understand any subsequent trends in the derived conversion factors.

Histograms of the tracer ratios are shown in Fig. 2, split by factors such as lensing, redshift, SFR, and other notable quantities. The correlations of the three tracer luminosities are shown in Fig. 3, where the various samples are colour coded and labelled and in each panel the blue line and shaded region represent the best fit and 2​σ2\sigma error interval. Fitting was performed using our own Orthogonal Distance Regression (ODR) method, which includes xx and yy errors, intrinsic scatter as a third parameter, and covariance in errors where required. The method is described in detail in Appendix I. Fit parameters, slope mm, intercept cc, and scatter ln λ\lambda , are listed in Table 4 and statistics for the various subsets from Fig. 2 are given in Table 5. It is instructive to look at these two plots together for the same luminosity pairs.

4.1 L850L_{850} vs. LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}

The left-hand column of Fig. 2 and Fig. 3(a) show the quantities L850L_{850} vs. LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}. There are no significant differences in the distribution of L850L_{850}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} with lensing, redshift or SF-mode, but the observed uncorrected ratio is significantly higher for galaxies with log LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} <8.9<8.9 (Fig. 2; left green histogram). These log LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} <8.9<8.9 galaxies tend to have optical disks dominated by atomic hydrogen (fH​If_{\rm H\,I} >1>1) and the likely increased contribution to L850L_{850} from dust associated with H i rather than H2 results in the offset to higher L850L_{850}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} ratios. For local galaxies with fH​If_{\rm H\,I} >1>1 we apply a correction (Appendix B.1) which appears to remove this offset (cyan diamonds in Fig. 3(a)). Galaxies with log LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} <8.9<8.9 from the VALES sample at 0.04<z<0.30.04<z<0.3 (Villanueva et al., 2017; Hughes et al., 2017) have noticeably higher L850L_{850}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} ratios than VALES galaxies with log LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} >8.9>8.9 (peach circles in Fig. 3(a) and Table 5). There are no published H i measurements for VALES, but we suspect that the lo-VALES sample with log LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} <8.9<8.9 is likely to be H i-rich, based on the similarity between the log LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} <8.9<8.9 and fH​If_{\rm H\,I} >1>1 categories in the third panel. We therefore exclude lo-VALES from our averages, as we suspect they are in need of a correction for H i but we have no means to apply one. We also recommend that a low LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} requires careful consideration of H i-related dust. In Fig. 3(a), the tracers show a linear dependence, regardless of exactly which galaxies are included (Table 4). The lo-VALES galaxies are excluded from all the fits.

4.2 L850L_{850} vs. LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}

The central column of Fig. 2 and Fig. 3(b) show L850L_{850} vs. LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}, the pair with the least scatter (ln⁡λ\ln\lambda in Table 4). There are no significant differences in the distributions of L850L_{850}/LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} as a function of lensing, redshift or SF-mode. The L850L_{850}–LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} sample has 12 galaxies with large angular sizes from J19 that have only part of their disk detected in C i, denoted C icor. To compare LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} and L850L_{850} for these galaxies, we need to apply an aperture correction to their C i fluxes, thereby assuming that their LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} ratios remain roughly constant across the disk (see Appendix 4.4). Some of the correction factors are very large (up to 0.7 dex); even after correction, their L850L_{850}/LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} ratios are significantly offset from the rest of the MS sample (green histogram). Fig. 3(b) shows L850L_{850} vs. LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}, with the C icor galaxies as pink diamonds. The fit to all galaxies including the C icor subset is shown as a dotted blue line, and has a sub-linear slope mm (3​σ3\sigma), although the difference is very small (m=0.937±0.020m=0.937\pm 0.020). Excluding the C icor galaxies from the fit leaves a linear relationship, shown by the blue solid line. At first glance, this and the green histogram in Fig. 2 suggest that our CO-based corrections are insufficient; however, Fig. 3(d) shows that the problem is not simply the assumption used to correct LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} to match the global L850L_{850}. This plot shows the dust emissivity cross-section, σ850′\sigma^{\prime}_{850}, equivalent to L850L_{850} but with the temperature sensitivity removed1818 18 σ850′\sigma^{\prime}_{850} is derived from the data provided in Jiao et al. (2021) by multiplying the dust mass in the C i aperture by the κ850\kappa_{850} used in their method, κ850\kappa_{850} = 0.034 m2 kg-1 (Draine, 2003; Draine et al., 2007).. Importantly, this quantity is measured in the same aperture as LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}. The C icor galaxies are shown as pink stars, and they – along with many other low-luminosity galaxies in J21 – still appear to have less C i emission for a given amount of dust.

4.3 LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} vs. LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}

The right-hand column of Fig. 2 and Fig. 3(c) show LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} vs. LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}. There are no significant differences in LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} for strongly lensed vs. unlensed sources, but the highest redshift, z>3z>3, galaxies have higher LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} ratios at marginal significance (p=0.012p=0.012). There are only 11 galaxies at z>3z>3 and a larger sample is needed to determine if this is a genuinely significant trend. Fig. 3(c) shows the C icor galaxies as pink diamonds, where the C i and CO fluxes are measured in the same apertures by J19. The solid line shows the fit to all galaxies, which is non-linear at 3σ\sigma significance (m=1.078±0.026m=1.078\pm 0.026). The slope becomes linear once the C icor galaxies are removed. The green histogram in Fig. 2 (right) shows more clearly why we see this: the C icor galaxies have significantly lower LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} ratios compared to other galaxies at similar or higher luminosity. The bottom histogram shows a marginal difference between galaxies with different SFRs (p=0.056p=0.056) when excluding the C icor galaxies, which becomes significant when they are included (p=0.006p=0.006).

4.4 Resolved C i fluxes from Herschel FTS mapping

The local resolved galaxies observed with Herschel FTS (Jiao et al., 2019) lie off the global trends seen in Fig. 3. There are possible physical explanations why lower luminosity, and more quiescently star-forming galaxies might have lower C i/CO line ratios (for example, different ISM environments in terms of their position in the CR energy density vs average molecular gas density diagram: see Figure 1 in Bisbas et al., 2015). Low ratios of LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} have been found in other studies, most intriguingly in the case of the interacting LIRG NGC 6052 using ALMA (Michiyama et al., 2020), and some high-zz strongly lensed sources (Harrington et al., 2021). Such ratios tend to be unusual in higher luminosity samples, however, whereas the resolved FTS sample has a very low average for the C i line ratios with both CO and dust.

We recommend caution in the interpretation of the data for these resolved FTS sources because another team subsequently presented the same data but drew different conclusions (Crocker et al., 2019). We can therefore only note that the C i fluxes from Herschel FTS mapping datasets are not always consistent when analysed by different teams.1919 19 Crocker et al. did not provide integrated fluxes, nor a method to determine them from their published measurements; hence, we cannot use their work directly in our analysis. Q. Jiao has provided us with the maps used in J19, enabling us to check the measurements independently and extend our analysis, but we have had no responses to our requests for integrated fluxes or the details of the method used from the Crocker team. As these resolved FTS measurements are essentially the only source of C i data at log LIR<11L_{\rm IR}<11, and carry a lot of weight in LIRL_{\rm IR} and SFR correlations, we chose not to include the C icor galaxies in the statistical analysis. If, instead, we take the J19 measurements at face value – they signpost a fundamental physical change in C i properties, a finding which clearly warrants further study with ground-based facilities. We discuss possible physical mechanisms for changes in the LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}and LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/L850L_{850} ratios in Appendix B.2.

4.5 Trends with global indicators of star-formation.

Finally, we check to see if any of the tracer ratios are sensitive to SFR indicators. In our data-set the dust observables LIRL_{\rm IR} and TdT_{\rm d} are indicators of the intensity and magnitude of star formation in galaxies (Kennicutt, 1998; Foyle et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2021, e.g.). As expected, the distribution of TdT_{\rm d} is very different for the MS galaxies and SMGs (Fig. 4 and Table 5), reflecting the increase in the intensity of star formation in the SMGs. The only tracer ratio sensitive to these SF indicators is LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}, which in Figure 5 is seen to increase with LIRL_{\rm IR} and TdT_{\rm d} when all galaxies are considered. Such a trend was not reported for smaller samples over a more limited range of luminosity (Jiao et al., 2017; Jiao et al., 2019, e.g.), presumably because of limited statistics. However, if the C icor galaxies (pink diamonds) are excluded, the correlation all but disappears (blue dotted line).

Naively, we might expect LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} to rise with increasing SFR intensity, due to the expected destruction of CO by cosmic rays (CR) in high-SFR environments (Bisbas et al., 2015, e.g.). For a given range of H2 densities in the typically hierarchical molecular clouds, any increased CR-induced ionisation rate, ζCR\zeta_{\rm CR} (due to a rising average CR energy density, UCRU_{\rm CR}) will destroy CO in the lower-density, more extended areas, while leaving CO still tracing H2 in the more compact, denser regions (see also Figure 1 of Papadopoulos et al., 2018 for a visual effect of this). Intriguingly, the gas density, nn(H2), and CR ionization rate, ζCR\zeta_{\rm CR}, will compete against each other in ULIRG/SMG environments, with the higher <n> expected in their highly turbulent ISM tending to keep the ordinary CO/C i chemistry in place, even when exposed to the higher ζCR\zeta_{\rm CR} values.2020 20 We here assume that CR energy density UCR∝ρSFRU_{\rm CR}\propto\rm\rho_{SFR} and CR ionisation rate ζCR∝UCR\mbox{$\zeta_{\rm CR}$}\propto U_{\rm CR}. Guessing which one will win this highly non-linear competition (see Fig 1, 8 in Bisbas et al., 2015) is dangerous in the absence of CO and C i line data. These effects have been probed with a variety of simulations (Bisbas et al., 2015; Bisbas et al., 2021; Clark et al., 2019a; Gong et al., 2020, e.g.) and while showing similar trends, they are not easily parameterisable in terms of nn(H2) and ζCR\zeta_{\rm CR}; one reason why such cross-calibration efforts of the available gas mass tracers are so important.2121 21 On an individual galaxy basis one could assemble well-sampled CO, 13CO and C i line SLEDs and overcome these problems with detailed analysis (Papadopoulos et al., 2014, e.g.). However, even in the ALMA era this remains very expensive in terms of telescope time making it prohibitive for large samples of galaxies.

The other two tracer ratios show no trends with either LIRL_{\rm IR}, TdT_{\rm d} (our proxies for SFR) – we present the relevant plots in Appendix 14 for completeness.

5 Results

In this section we present the results of the optimisation method, firstly for the daX sample, for which we have all three gas tracers, and later for the other three samples, for which we have pairs of tracers. We investigate trends of the conversion factors with LIRL_{\rm IR} and SFR. Mean values for the conversion factors are listed in Table 6.

Fig. 6 shows the results for the daX sample (Figs 7–9 present the same results for each of the samples in turn). The top row of each plot shows the distribution of the relevant physical parameter for C i and dust, and the conversion factor for CO: XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}, κH\kappa_{\rm H} and αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}. The lower left panels show the same quantities for the individual galaxies as a function of LIRL_{\rm IR}; each panel indicates a reference measure to give context. For XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}, the horizontal lines indicate the measured extremes found in the local Universe: Orion A/B clouds in the Milky Way (Ikeda et al., 2002) and the starburst centre of M 82 (White et al., 1994), while the grey shaded region shows the range of values inferred from observations of GRB hosts and QSO absorbers for solar metallicity by Heintz & Watson (2020). They use a method which does not rely on emission measures of dust, CO or C i and so can be considered independent. For αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}, the horizontal lines indicate the typical αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} for the Milky Way (Bolatto et al., 2013) and that commonly adopted2222 22 In this panel, αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} does not include the factor 1.36 for He. for ULIRGs and SMGs (Downes & Solomon, 1998). For κH\kappa_{\rm H}, we show a shaded band indicating the range derived for local galaxies (see Table 15), along with lines showing the value for the most diffuse and dense sight lines in the Milky Way (Remy et al., 2017). The right lower panels show the running log-means as a function of LIRL_{\rm IR} to make it easier to see any trends, and additionally includes2323 23 As elsewhere, the empirical parameters αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} and α850\alpha_{850} include the factor 1.36 for He. the empirical parameters, αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} and α850\alpha_{850}. The solid shaded bins are the means for the grey points, which are those used to determine the calibration; the yellow points are C icor and the semi-transparent pentagon is the mean of those – see §4.4 for more details.

Fig. 6 shows that for galaxies with log LIR>11L_{\rm IR}>11 there are only weak trends of the conversion factors with LIRL_{\rm IR}. While the normalisation (κHN=1884\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}^{\rm N}=1884 kg m-2) was chosen to produce average dust properties consistent with the Milky Way and other nearby spirals, the CO and C i conversion factors derived from the luminosity ratios also lie within the ranges expected from independent studies. The averages at log LIR<11L_{\rm IR}<11 are based on only a small number of points (12) and more C i studies are required to probe quiescent local galaxies.

5.1 A calibration for the gas masses

We next give a prescription for estimating gas mass, tailored to how many tracers are available and – where appropriate – the type of galaxy being investigated.

5.1.1 Dual-band

While the information content is greatest for the daX sample, which has three tracer pairs to optimise, the method presented in §3 still improves the cross-calibration for samples which have two tracer measurements, i.e. one pair. The results for the Xd, Xa and ad samples are shown in Figs 7–9 and behave similarly to the daX sample, as one would hope given that the daX galaxies are a subset of the others. The pink diamonds in the lower-left panels in Figs 7 and 8 denote the C icor galaxies. The cyan diamonds in the lower-left panel of Fig. 9 are galaxies with fH​If_{\rm H\,I}>1 which have been corrected for the contribution of dust mixed with the H i gas, as described in Appendix A. The open peach circles are the lo-VALES galaxies, which we suspect to have fH​If_{\rm H\,I}>1 (see §4.1) but which we cannot correct. We do not include these in any averages or histograms.

The method previously used in the literature (Alaghband-Zadeh et al., 2013; Scoville et al., 2016; Orellana et al., 2017; Hughes et al., 2017; Valentino et al., 2018, e.g.) has been to assume one tracer in a pair (e.g. LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}) has a known conversion (αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}), then to fix that factor for all galaxies in order to estimate the second (i.e. the one of interest). We show this simple method alongside our optimal method as grey lines and dashed grey error bars in the relevant panels of Figs 7–9. The scatter in the conversion factors for the optimised estimates are governed by the intrinsic scatter we inferred in our analysis of the data in Appendix E, free of assumptions. In contrast, the simple method proscribes that there is no scatter in the known conversion factor, and therefore all of the intrinsic scatter in the luminosity ratio is attributed to the second conversion factor of interest. The optimised method presented here does not assume an ad hoc preference for any particular conversion factor: as it is based on empirical variance analysis, it uses more of the available information to improve the accuracy of the estimated conversion factors. The histograms in Figs (7–9) show that the scatter in the factor of interest is larger when using the simple method, and the trends in the running medians are also more exaggerated.

Comparing the parameter estimates using three tracers to those using two tracers for the same galaxies allows us to test the accuracy of these two-tracer estimates. The details are in Appendix H, but in summary there is a reasonable correlation between the three-tracer and two-tracer estimates, without bias (Fig. 15) and an average scatter of 0.06–0.08 dex.

Thus, when multiple H2 tracers are available, we recommend the procedure outlined in the example below.

Example:

Take the example of a galaxy with observations of both dust and CO. We take the mean value for the appropriate pair combination from Table 3: αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}/κH\kappa_{\rm H}=0.00133. For our adopted sample mean normalisation of κN=1884\kappa^{\rm N}=1884 kg m-2, we now infer the sample mean expectation value of ⟨α⟩=0.00133×1884=2.5\langle\alpha\rangle=0.00133\times 1884=2.5 (excluding He). The sample means, κN\kappa^{\rm N} (assumed) and ⟨α⟩\langle\alpha\rangle (derived), are next used to estimate an initial gas mass for our galaxy in each of the two tracers, L850L_{850} and LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}.

Mκ=κN​L850/4​π​B​(ν850,Tmw)Mα=⟨α⟩​LCO′M_{\kappa}=\kappa^{\rm N}\mbox{$L_{850}$}/4\pi B(\nu_{850},\mbox{$T_{\rm mw}$})\\ M_{\alpha}=\langle\alpha\rangle\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$}\\ (18)

Next, we calculate the effective standard deviation by adding the observational error on the tracer luminosities in quadrature to the intrinsic scatter for α\alpha and κ\kappa.

σeffκ=sκ2+σ8502σeffα=sα2+σCO2\sigma^{\kappa}_{\rm eff}=\sqrt{s_{\kappa}^{2}+\sigma_{850}^{2}}\\ \sigma^{\alpha}_{\rm eff}=\sqrt{s_{\alpha}^{2}+\sigma_{\rm CO}^{2}}\\ (19)

where σ850\sigma_{850}, σCO\sigma_{\rm CO} are the errors on log⁡(L850)\log(\mbox{$L_{850}$}) and log⁡(LCO′)\log(\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$}), and sκs_{\kappa} and sαs_{\alpha} are the intrinsic scatter on log⁡(κH)\log(\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}) and log⁡(αCO)\log(\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}) listed in Table 3. The optimal H2 mass estimate is then calculated thus:

Mopt=Mκ/σκ,eff2+Mα/σα,eff21/σκ,eff2+1/σα,eff2M^{\rm opt}=\frac{M_{\kappa}/\sigma^{2}_{\rm\kappa,eff}+M_{\alpha}/\sigma^{2}_{\rm\alpha,eff}}{1/\sigma^{2}_{\rm\kappa,eff}+1/\sigma^{2}_{\rm\alpha,eff}} (20)

We now work back to find the optimal conversion parameters for this galaxy:

κHopt=κN​Mopt/MκαCOopt=⟨α⟩​Mopt/Mα.\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}^{\rm opt}=\kappa^{\rm N}M^{\rm opt}/M_{\kappa}\\ \mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}^{\rm opt}=\langle\alpha\rangle M^{\rm opt}/M_{\alpha}.\\ (21)

5.1.2 Single band: empirical conversion factors

The three empirical conversion factors, α850\alpha_{850}, αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} and αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}, directly relate the observable tracer luminosity to a gas mass, according to Eqn. 1. If only one tracer (LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}, LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} or L850L_{850}) is available, the empirical conversion factor we have estimated in Table 7 is the best choice.
