We adopt a convention that the empirical parameters are referenced to MmolM_{\rm mol}, which includes a factor 1.36 for He.

Figs 6–9 show the empirical conversion factors as a function of LIRL_{\rm IR}; Fig. 10 shows the empirical conversion factors as a function of the tracer luminosity, and Fig. 11 shows their distribution when the sample is split into MS galaxies and SMGs (see Table 8 for details). All empirical factors show significant but shallow correlations with the tracer luminosity. We have carefully accounted for the co-variance between the xx and yy parameters when fitting, so the correlations we find are not caused by the involvement2424 24 The inclusion of the co-variance matrix in the fit reduces the slope (closer to zero) by 0.05. of L850L_{850}, LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} and LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} in the derivation of α850\alpha_{850}, αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} and αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}. Table 9 lists the fit parameters. The intrinsic scatter in all of these relationships is very small once the measurement errors are accounted for. Correlations are also seen between LIRL_{\rm IR} and α850\alpha_{850}, αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} and αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}(Fig. 7–9), albeit with more scatter.

A correlation between α850\alpha_{850} and L850L_{850} was also noted by Sco16 (shown as the red dashed line on our plot) but ours is somewhat shallower (m=0.052m=0.052 vs m=0.07m=0.07 from Sco16), although the difference is unlikely2525 25 Sco16 do not quote an error on their fit, so it is difficult to be certain, but the error on Sco16 would likely be larger than ours, which means they are consistent to within 2σ\sigma. to be significant. These shallow but significant relationships with their tracer luminosity could be further applied to give more accurate calibration (see Table 9). The trends of αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} and αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} with their respective tracers are explored for the first time in large numbers here.

5.2 Discussion of empirical factors relative to the literature.

5.2.1 Submillimetre dust empirical calibration, α850\alpha_{850}

The final calibration factors from this work are provided in Table 10. A compilation of α850\alpha_{850} values from our optimal method2626 26 There is no significant difference if we fix αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} to 4.3. and those from the literature, referenced to a common αCO=4.3\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=4.3: the Galactic value including He from Bolatto et al., 2013) is presented in Table 11. Literature values cover the range, α850\alpha_{850} = 3.6–10.1×101210.1\times 10^{12}, comfortably within the range of estimates here: α850opt=\mbox{$\alpha_{850}$}^{\rm opt}= 6.5–7.2×10127.2\times 10^{12}. The lowest value, α850=3.6−1.9+3.6×1012\mbox{$\alpha_{850}$}=3.6^{+3.6}_{-1.9}\times 10^{12}, comes from the local sample of Orellana et al. (2017), who include H i as well as MmolM_{\rm mol} (from LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}). Their α850\alpha_{850} refers to the total gas mass – sensibly, since their lower luminosity sample is more H i-dominated than the others we compare to – meaning that a lower value for α850\alpha_{850} is required. The highest value, α850=(10.1±0.3)×1012\mbox{$\alpha_{850}$}=(10.1\pm 0.3)\times 10^{12}, is from Sco16.2727 27 The original value of α850=6.7×1012\mbox{$\alpha_{850}$}=6.7\times 10^{12} quoted by Sco16 assumed that αCO=6.5\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=6.5 to calibrate the gas mass from CO. Re-normalising the Sco16 result to the same αCO=4.3\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=4.3 as our literature comparison increases the Sco16 value to α850​(αCO=4.3)=10.1×1012\mbox{$\alpha_{850}$}({\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=4.3})=10.1\times 10^{12}. There are two reasons why Sco16 found a significantly higher α850\alpha_{850} compared to our analysis. The first is simple mathematics, as Sco16 quote a linear mean for a distribution that has a significant tail to higher values; in contrast, we quote a log-mean which is less sensitive to tails. This statistical bias results in a linear mean for α850\alpha_{850} which is 20 per cent higher than the log-mean (Behroozi et al., 2013) . Assuming the shape of our α850\alpha_{850} distribution is similar to that from Sco16, we adjust their linear mean down by 20 per cent to approximate our log-mean method. Thus our log-mean estimate of the Sco16 value is α850LM​(Sco16)=8.4×1012\mbox{$\alpha_{850}$}^{\rm LM}(\rm Sco16)=8.4\times 10^{12}. Secondly, there have been changes in the versions of the Herschel pipeline data used as the basis for the local portion of the Sco16 sample (see Appendix A). When we re-fitted the local galaxy SEDs to estimate TmwT_{\rm mw} and L850L_{850} using the most recent Herschel flux densities (Chu et al., 2017; Clark et al., 2018) we found an increase in L850L_{850} of ∼0.1\sim 0.1 dex compared to that reported in Sco162828 28 This difference is not just the photometry change; Sco16 used a different method to estimate L850L_{850} from the Herschel 500-μ\mum fluxes.. Once these factors are accounted for, the Sco16 result is comparable to ours.

Atomic carbon empirical factor: αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I}

We compare our optimised αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} estimates with others from the literature in Table 12, and for reference we also compile the literature values for XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} in Table 13, the two are related simply by the excitation factor Q10Q_{10}, as given in Eqn. 11. Our values are a weighted average of the three samples that contain C i, where we find ⟨αC​I⟩=17.3±0.3\langle\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}\rangle=17.3\pm 0.3 (standard error on the mean). This compares well with the only truly independent measure, αC​I=21.4−8+13\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}=21.4^{+13}_{-8}, from absorber systems across a range of redshift by Heintz & Watson (2020), but is considerably higher than reported by many literature studies, e.g. αC​I=4.9\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}=4.9–10.3 for a large study of (U)LIRGs by Jiao et al., 2017 and αC​I=7.3−3.6+6.9\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}=7.3^{+6.9}_{-3.6} for local disks by Crocker et al. (2019). Many literature studies assume a fixed value for either XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} or αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} in order to derive αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} (typically XC​I=3×10−5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}=3\times 10^{-5} or αCO=1\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=1 for high-zz SMG or local (U)LIRGs). These assumed values are very different from those we have derived here under our minimal assumption that metal rich galaxies have similar dust properties. Table 12 describes the assumptions made for each literature source.

The MS galaxies in this work have a value of αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} of 19.1±0.619.1\pm 0.6, again significantly higher than that found in Crocker et al. (2019). However, J19, using a largely overlapping sample, derived a value of αC​I=19.9±1.9\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}=19.9\pm 1.9 using the same Herschel FTS C i mapping observations. Crocker et al. use L[CO]​(2−1)′L^{\prime}_{\rm[CO](2-1)} images and spatially resolved αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} estimates from Sandstrom et al. (2013), which were derived using a robust method which minimises the scatter in the gas-to-dust ratio (see also Eales et al., 2012). While there are no a priori assumptions about αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} in Crocker et al. (2019), implicit assumptions are required for the average CO r21r_{21} excitation. The limited sensitivity of the FTS instrument to [C i](1–0) meant that C i was primarily detected in the brighter nuclear regions, where αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} tends to be lower than is typical in spiral disks (∼1\sim 1 compared to ∼3\sim 3–4), (Sandstrom et al., 2013, e.g.) – as noted by Crocker et al. Their measured LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} ratios in the resolved regions are compatible with other MS galaxies in our sample (though still higher than the ratios derived for the same set of sources by J19, see Fig. 5), meaning that the αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I}/αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} ratios are also similar. As αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} in these regions is determined to be low in the Sandstrom et al. (2013) analysis, the αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} inferred by Crocker et al. is correspondingly lower as well.

Jiao et al. (2021) (henceforth J21) use CO(1–0), H i, [C i](1–0), dust continuum and metallicity maps to investigate the variation of αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} and αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} across the disks of six well-resolved local galaxies from their J19 study. They use the FIR/submm dust maps from Spitzer and Herschel and the method of Draine et al. (2007) to model the dust mass across the galaxy and relate this to a gas mass via a relationship between dust-to-gas and metallicity (Muñoz-Mateos et al., 2009; Draine et al., 2007; Sandstrom et al., 2013). As they explicitly use the dust mass together with a model of the δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR} dependence on metallicity, their results are normalised to the dust properties of the Draine & Li (2007) model (hereafter 77), which assumes δGDR=100\mbox{$\delta_{\rm GDR}$}=100 and κ850=0.034\mbox{$\kappa_{850}$}=0.034 m2 kg-1 at solar metallicity. Their self-consistent DGR(ii) method derives weighted mean values of ⟨αC​I⟩=19.9±1.9\langle\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}\rangle=19.9\pm 1.9 (including the information from lower limits) and ⟨αCO⟩=2.0±0.3\langle\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}\rangle=2.0\pm 0.3 (2.6±0.42.6\pm 0.4) over the same area as the C i observations (the entire CO detection region)2929 29 We have multiplied the values in J21 by 1.36 to include He for consistency with our convention.. In the central region, the αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} values are significantly lower at αCOC=1.5±0.3\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}^{\rm C}=1.5\pm 0.3, while αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} is not found to be significantly different with αC​IC=21.8±0.5\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}^{\rm C}=21.8\pm 0.5. These values are comparable to to our average of αC​I=19.1±0.6\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}=19.1\pm 0.6 for MS galaxies, and to the average value for Z⊙Z_{\odot} derived independently by Heintz & Watson (2020) of αC​I​(HW20)=21.4−8.2+13.3\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}(\rm HW20)=21.4^{+13.3}_{-8.2}3030 30 While there are differences in the normalisation for the dust mass model chosen by J21 and ourselves, the introduction of a metallicity dependence for the dust-to-gas ratio by J21 means that there is no simple way to scale their results to our method. However, we can calculate their average ‘effective κH\kappa_{\rm H}’, κeff=1300\kappa_{\rm eff}=1300, which indicates that J21 derive a lower H2 for a given L850L_{850} compared to our normalisation (and hence a lower value of αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} and αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}). However, the six galaxies in J21 are a subset of the C icor objects, at the low luminosity end where there are potential decreases in κH\kappa_{\rm H} and increases in αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I}..

CO empirical factor: αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}

We compare our optimised αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} estimates with others from the literature in Table 14. Sophisticated LVG modelling with very large datasets which include high-density gas tracers, optically thin CO isotopologues, full CO SLEDs, and sometimes the C i lines and dust emission (Weiß et al., 2007; Papadopoulos et al., 2012b; Papadopoulos et al., 2014; Israel, 2020; Harrington et al., 2021, e.g.) can break some of the model degeneracies of the optically thick CO lines, though the method is still reliant on assumptions for [CO/H2], isotopologue ratios, the number of components allowed (single components give very different results to multiple components) and the allowed range of velocity gradients in the models.

The best examples are NGC 6240 (Papadopoulos et al., 2014) and the Planck lensed galaxies (Harrington et al., 2021) where detailed LVG modelling and comprehensive datasets have sufficient constraints to break the degeneracies which usually be-devil this method. The two-component LVG result for NGC 6240 is αCO=2\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=2–4 (Papadopoulos et al., 2014) (cf. αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}=0.6 when using a single component LVG model Papadopoulos et al., 2012b) and we can further use the ratio of LC​I′/LCO′\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}$}/\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$} measured by Cicone et al. (2018) and our relationship, LC​I′/LCO′=αCO/αC​I=3324​αCOXC​I\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}$}/\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$}=\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}/\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}=3324\,\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}, to infer that XC​I=1.4\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}=1.4–2.9×10−52.9\times 10^{-5} in the starburst region. In fact, our optimised values for this galaxy using global fluxes, are αCO​(daX)=2.9±0.6\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}({\rm daX})=2.9\pm 0.6, XC​I​(daX)=(2.4±0.5)×10−5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}({\rm daX})=(2.4\pm 0.5)\times 10^{-5}, κH​(daX)=2800±700\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}({\rm daX})=2800\pm 700 (δGDR=200\mbox{$\delta_{\rm GDR}$}=200), in excellent agreement. The Planck lensed galaxies analysed by Harrington et al. (2021) do not have the same degeneracy-breaking lines used by (Papadopoulos et al., 2014) in their analysis, but they do have multi-JJ CO coverage and incorporate the C i lines and the dust continuum emission in their model fitting, based on Weiß et al. (2007). They assume similar dust parameters as we do for their normalisations (δGDR=120\mbox{$\delta_{\rm GDR}$}=120–150 with κ850=0.08\mbox{$\kappa_{850}$}=0.08 m2 kg-1). With this, they infer an average αCO=3\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=3–4 and an average αC​I=16.2±7.9\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}=16.2\pm 7.9 (incl. He), remarkably consistent with our results, given our very simple approach.

5.3 Lack of bi-modality in the conversion factors

Our sample contains normal star forming galaxies – those obeying the SFR–M⋆M_{\star} correlation that forms as a result of the more intimate relationship between SFR and H2 – as well as many extreme star-forming systems, which belong to the (U)LIRG and high-zz submillimeter selected samples. Here we remind the reader that we refer to the extreme SF group – those that supposedly require a lower αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} – as ‘SMGs’, and the normal star forming sources as ‘MS galaxies’, or sometimes just ‘MS’. As mentioned in Section 2, the assignment of the galaxies to either category is by nature of the data rather ‘fuzzy’ as we do not have a measure of SFR or stellar mass for all sources, nor any homogeneous way to estimate them. We thus rely on the categories used by previous authors where possible, especially for high-zz sources. The z=1z=1 galaxies from the samples of Bourne et al. (2019); Valentino et al. (2018); Valentino et al. (2020) are deemed to be ‘MS’, as are the sources from ASPECs (Boogaard et al., 2020). Most low redshift sources with log LIRL_{\rm IR}<12 are classed as ‘MS’ though there are some exceptional LIRG class sources in the local Universe which have extreme properties as evidenced by their FIR, MIR lines and vibrational HCN (Díaz-Santos et al., 2017; Falstad et al., 2021). We note that using a more conservative separation when assigning galaxies into MS and extreme starburst categories does not change any of the results. We therefore conclude that while our assignment of sources into the two SF categories is not perfect, this categorisation is not capable of masking any strong bi-modality in the observable ratios.

Fig. 11 and Table 8 detail the distributions of conversion factors for each sample, split into MS galaxies and SMGs. While formally there are significant differences in the parameters for some samples, these are very small – around 10–20 per cent in the mean, rather than the factor ∼3\sim 3–4×4\times often assumed for αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} (e.g. Downes & Solomon, 1998, αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}=0.8, derived for four ULIRGs). In fact, only the ad sample shows any difference in αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} between the MS galaxies and SMGs, while the estimates based on C i and CO, or on all three tracers, show no significant difference. This is partially explained by the larger luminosity range in the ad sample, combined with the previously noted negative correlation between αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} and luminosity (Figs 9 and 10), with a factor ∼2×\sim 2\times reduction in αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} for a factor ∼100×\sim 100\times increase in LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}. We cannot rule out that the correlation of αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} with luminosity is the true reason that the ad sample shows a significant difference between MS galaxies and SMGs3131 31 LIR​(ad)​(MS)=10.95\mbox{$L_{\rm IR}$}{\rm(ad)}{\rm(MS)}=10.95 (LCO′​(ad)​(MS)=9.31\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$}{\rm(ad)}{\rm(MS)}=9.31) while LIR​(Xa)​(MS)=11.22\mbox{$L_{\rm IR}$}{\rm(Xa)}{\rm(MS)}=11.22 (LCO′​(Xa)​(MS)=9.52\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$}{\rm(Xa)}{\rm(MS)}=9.52). Using the relation in Table 9, the expected Δ​αCO=αCO​(MS)−αCO​(SMG)=0.36\Delta\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}{\rm(MS)}-\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}{\rm(SMG)}=0.36 for the Xa sample and – due to the lower numbers in the Xa and daX samples – such a difference would not be detected at a significant level, if it existed..

This is not the first time3232 32 However our current dataset is more homogeneous, using only CO(1–0) or CO(2–1) and a consistent approach to modelling the dust with our empirical relations for TmwT_{\rm mw}. that lack of bi-modality in αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} has been reported when compared to dust-based determinations (Magdis et al., 2012; Rowlands et al., 2014; Genzel et al., 2015, e.g.). The range of αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} we find for SMGs (see Fig. 9) is well within the framework set out by Papadopoulos et al. (2012a), who noted that galaxies with a highly turbulent ISM (e.g. ULIRGs and SMGs) can have αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} similar to galaxies with a much more quiescent ISM, the only difference being that in a turbulent ISM, the distribution of gas mass as a function of density is weighted to higher densities than in a less-turbulent ISM.

Recent joint SLED/SED modelling of an exquisite dataset that includes CO, C i and dust continuum for lensed SMGs (Harrington et al., 2021) finds a mean αCO=3.4\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=3.4–4.2 for these highly turbulent galaxies (albeit with a large dispersion). The Harrington et al. radiative transfer models employ a continuum distribution of molecular gas mass as a function of average Mach number (and average density of the molecular cloud ensemble), making them better equipped to ‘capture’ any re-distribution of the underlying molecular gas mass towards higher densities. While important for other issues (e.g. the initial conditions of star formation in SMGs/ULIRGs), such a re-distribution in a highly turbulent ISM may actually leave αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} statistically unaffected. The initial reports of a bimodal αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} factor in the local Universe, with ∼\sim4-5×\times lower values for ULIRGs than LIRGs and ordinary spirals, can possibly be explained by a CO-luminous, strongly unbound, low-density molecular gas component found preferentially in ULIRGs. Such a component can dominate the global CO(1–0) line luminosities of ULIRGs/SMGs (even if containing only small fractions of their total molecular gas), while its large Kvir\rm K_{vir} values will yield systematically low αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} factors, under one-component LVG modelling (Equation 9).3333 33 Also we must consider the size of the original sample – four ULIRGs in the first study by Downes & Solomon (1998).

For individual galaxies, only multi-component models of SLED/SED (that also include molecules/transitions tracing the dense gas) can properly account for this effect (Papadopoulos et al., 2014; Harrington et al., 2021, e.g.), while for large galaxy samples, our cross-calibration of αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} against the other two molecular gas mass tracers, is the most economical method. In that regard it is worth noting that dust continuum is immune to the gas-dynamics effects described above, i.e. a diffuse low-density, unbound, H2\rm H_{2} gas component will contribute very little to the total dust continuum if its gas/dust mass is indeed low. The optically thin C i line emission will also be much less sensitive than CO(1–0) to such gas-dynamics effects exactly because of its low optical depths. These are perhaps the reasons why our cross-calibration of αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} against dust and C i emission has not uncovered any obvious bimodality of its values in MS galaxies compared to SMGs.

The range of values we find for αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} is consistent with expected values for Z>0.5​Z⊙Z>0.5\,Z_{\odot} galaxies (Accurso et al. 2017, based on calibrating αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} using Cii). Using their predictions, we would expect 2.7<αCO<15.22.7<\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}<15.2 for the likely range of metallicity and offset from the MS in our sample.

Our underlying assumption: that the dust–gas properties of MS galaxies and SMGs can be described as a uni-modal distribution with well defined mean and scatter, is based on our finding that the luminosity ratios (Fig. 2) – the most basic observables used in deriving the empirical conversion factors – have such a distribution. They show no evidence for the strong bi-modality advocated for αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} in some of the literature. That the distribution of the observed luminosity ratio is, to first order, similar to the distribution of the conversion parameters, is the simplest ‘Occam’s Razor’ assumption we can make.

To see what a different initial assumption would mean for the conversion factors, we repeated our analysis, this time inserting the popular bi-modal behaviour in αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} (Greve et al., 2005; Weiß et al., 2005; Tacconi et al., 2006; Tacconi et al., 2008; Genzel et al., 2010; Walter et al., 2011; Alaghband-Zadeh et al., 2013; Jiao et al., 2017; Valentino et al., 2018) as our prior, such that the sample mean normalisations for SMGs and MS galaxies are set to be different: αCON​(SMG)=0.8\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}^{\rm N}(\rm SMG)=0.8 and κHN​(MS)=1884\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}^{\rm N}(\rm MS)=1884 kg m-2. Our optimal method then allows the data to return the most likely values for the other parameters3434 34 We did not re-calculate the intrinsic scatter split into MS galaxies and SMGs, only the values of the XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}/αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} and αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I}/κH\kappa_{\rm H} pairs. under these assumptions.

Fig. 12 shows the results with this bi-modal normalisation, (blue points: MS galaxies, red points: SMGs). By design, we have reproduced the extreme bi-modality αCO​(MS)∼3\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}(\rm MS)\sim 3–4 and αCO​(SMG)∼1\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}(\rm SMG)\sim 1, but Fig. 12 clearly shows that the same extreme bi-modality has to be present in κH\kappa_{\rm H} (δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}) and XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}, giving a clear prediction that XC​I​(SMG)≥4×10−5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}(\rm SMG)\geq 4\times 10^{-5} if the bimodality in αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} really exists, with essentially no overlap in XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} between the MS galaxies and SMGs. To test this will require an independent determination of XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} in SMGs, without reference to dust or CO calibration. To date, there is no such determination of XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}, although Izumi et al. (2020) observed the nearby LIRG NGC 7469 with ALMA, using kinematic data to derive Mdyn\rm{M_{dyn}}, which is the sum of MH2M_{\rm H2}, stellar mass and dark matter. This method has promise, but the systematic uncertainties in MH2M_{\rm H2} from this analysis are too large (0.3 dex) to answer our question. While the Izumi et al. study clearly indicates3535 35 via the extremely high observable ratio LC​I′/LCO′=0.92\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}$}/\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$}=0.92 in the CND that the [C0/CO\rm{C^{0}}/CO] abundance can be enhanced in extreme environments, the CND is only a tiny region and the global ratio for this source is very similar to other LIRGs, with LC​I′/LCO′=0.20±0.04\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}$}/\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$}=0.20\pm 0.04. Any study which wishes to test the bi-modality hypothesis must also be representative of the galaxy global properties.

Here we must stress again that for individual galaxies, joint SLED/SED radiative transfer models of well-sampled SLEDs and dust emission SEDs do recover Galactic-valued αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} factors even in (U)LIRGs or SMGs (Papadopoulos et al., 2014; Harrington et al., 2021). However such results cannot be used in a statistical sense, i.e. as typical of the respective galaxy populations for obvious reasons, and our statistical approach remains the sole avenue.

Indeed, the only way that a bi-modal αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} for MS galaxies and SMGs can be reconciled with MH2M_{\rm H2} estimates using dust or C i is to impose the same bi-modality on their conversion parameters (κH\kappa_{\rm H}, XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}, α850\alpha_{850}, αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I}). A reduction of αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} by a factor 3×3\times necessitates a decrease [increase] in κH\kappa_{\rm H} [XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}] by the same factor. Thus, if αCO=0.8\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=0.8 is preferred for extreme star-forming galaxies (Walter et al., 2011, e.g.), then κH=600\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}=600 (δGDR=43\mbox{$\delta_{\rm GDR}$}=43 for κ850=0.071\mbox{$\kappa_{850}$}=0.071 m2 kg-1) and XC​I=5.3×10−5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}=5.3\times 10^{-5} must also be adopted (statistically, for this galaxy population). This discrepancy was previously noted by Bothwell et al. (2017) and Valentino et al. (2018) who found that using XC​I​(SMG)=3×10−5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}(\rm SMG)=3\times 10^{-5} with LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} as a tracer resulted in larger gas masses than using LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} with the ‘ULIRG’ value of αCO=0.8\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=0.8. Therefore, the popular ‘choices’ of αCO=0.8\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=0.8 and XC​I=3×10−5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}=3\times 10^{-5} are incompatible with each other.

Based on our current understanding, there are two plausible physical mechanisms which may cause an increase in XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} and a decrease in κH\kappa_{\rm H} in extreme ISM conditions. The effect of enhanced cosmic ray densities on carbon chemistry (Bisbas et al., 2015; Bisbas et al., 2021; Glover & Clark, 2016; Gong et al., 2020) favour a higher [C0/CO]\rm[C^{0}/CO] abundance, however, this mechanism is density dependent and is less effective in dense regions, which typify the ISM of SMGs. Thus while extreme environments with elevated cosmic rays or X-rays would certainly act to increase XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} at a fixed density, it does not simply follow that extreme SF activity will produce high XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} since those same regions (CRDR/XDR) are typically found in regions with increased density.

The higher dense gas fractions common in SMGs may favour higher rates of grain growth, or mantling, both of which would reduce the value of κH\kappa_{\rm H} – i) by decreasing the δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR} and ii) by increasing the dust emissivity, κ850\kappa_{850}. Our results imply, however, that any such changes must act in harmony with each other so as to maintain the same observable ratios, so an increase in XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} must correlate directly with a decrease in κH\kappa_{\rm H} and αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}. This prediction is a clear challenge to models, and full astro-chemical simulations for the extreme physical conditions expected in the ISM of SMGs and ULIRGs will be needed to explore how the three tracers can vary in the exact same way through very different physical mechanisms.

5.4 On the robustness of our choices

5.4.1 Impact of uncorrected fH​If_{\rm H\,I}>1 galaxies

Statistically, the effect of having uncorrected fH​If_{\rm H\,I}>1 galaxies is small, since there are only 15 such galaxies, where ⟨αCO⟩\langle\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}\rangle increases3636 36 Note that this offset is linear, not logarithmic. by +0.27 in their luminosity bin compared to when they are removed altogether (by +0.18 compared to when they have been corrected). We are thus confident that dust associated with H i is not biasing our overall determination of conversion factors and their trends, at least in this sample. For individual galaxies, however, the difference in αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} can be very large. When using this method for low-redshift galaxies with significant H i within the dust-emitting region, corrections are needed.

5.4.2 Impact of using a constant TmwT_{\rm mw}

The strong correlation found between TmwT_{\rm mw} and luminosity (Fig. 1) has not been considered in previous works. In Appendix H.2, we show a comparison of results using our empirical TmwT_{\rm mw} relations to those for constant, TmwT_{\rm mw}=25 k. Summarising these findings:

  1. 1.

    The median offsets between parameters when using constant vs. variable TmwT_{\rm mw} are <0.015<0.015 dex. The scatter in a parameter is generally within 0.1 dex (Fig. 16). Thus the global averages we present in this paper are not affected by a change to constant TmwT_{\rm mw}=25 k.

  2. 2.

    Allowing TmwT_{\rm mw} to vary with LIRL_{\rm IR} is more realistic and leads to a shallow but significant trend with luminosity, such that αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} decreases with increasing LIRL_{\rm IR}, while κH\kappa_{\rm H}, α850\alpha_{850} and XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} increase slightly. Using a constant TmwT_{\rm mw} of 25 k produces no trends of any conversion factor with LIRL_{\rm IR} (Fig. 17).

  3. 3.

    Using a constant TmwT_{\rm mw} of 25 k results in gas masses up to 0.1 dex lower at log LIR<11L_{\rm IR}<11 and 0.1 dex higher at lIR<12.0l_{\rm IR}<12.0 compared to the variable TmwT_{\rm mw} used in the main analysis (Fig. 18).

6 Discussion

The diverse galaxies in this study show a remarkable consistency in their gas mass tracers, with linear relationships between all three pairs of observables, L850L_{850}, LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} and LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}.

We find weak trends in the conversion factors with LIRL_{\rm IR}; decreasing αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}, αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} and increasing α850\alpha_{850}, κH\kappa_{\rm H}, XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}. These trends are very shallow, amounting to a factor <2×<2\times change over 2–3 orders of magnitude in luminosity. The intrinsic variation in κH\kappa_{\rm H} and XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} (the physical quantities encompassing most of the uncertainties in the corresponding conversion factors) is likely very small, and approximating them with a single constant value should be robust. For the sub-samples with a C i tracer (daX, Xa, Xd), we see decreases in all three tracer conversion factors at log LIR<11L_{\rm IR}<11: XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} (15–25 per cent), αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} (10–30 per cent) and κH\kappa_{\rm H} (δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}: 20–25 per cent). However, the data indicating a drop in conversion factors originates from the J19 sample (see earlier discussions). More C i studies of normal star-forming galaxies in the local Universe are urgently required to further explore any such trend, in particular using the global C i line emission, rather than that of the central few kpc of a galaxy.

The average values of XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}, αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} and κH\kappa_{\rm H} (δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}) for galaxies with all three tracers (the daX sample) and log LIR>11L_{\rm IR}>11 are our ‘reference’ values, αCOR=3.7\mbox{$\alpha^{\rm R}_{\rm CO}$}=3.7 (including He), XC​IR=1.6×10−5\mbox{$X^{\rm R}_{\rm C\,I}$}=1.6\times 10^{-5}, κHR=1990​(δGDRR=141)\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}^{\rm R}=1990\,(\mbox{$\delta^{\rm R}_{\rm GDR}$}=141). These agree within the errors with the mean values determined using only two tracers. These reference values are not unique because only the ratios and products of the conversion factors are constrained by the observables, LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}, LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/L850L_{850} and L850L_{850}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}.

Once a conversion factor is known or assumed, however, the others can be determined by the self-consistent ratios listed in Table 3. For example, using the ad sub-sample and normalising to κHN=2800​m2​kg−1\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}^{\rm N}=2800\,\rm m^{2}\,kg^{-1} would produce XC​I=1.1×10−5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}=1.1\times 10^{-5} and αCO=4.7\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=4.7, in reasonable agreement with Accurso et al. (2017) for Z=0.6​Z⊙Z=0.6\,Z_{\odot}, while normalising to αCON=0.8\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}^{\rm N}=0.8 gives XC​I=5.8×10−5\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}=5.8\times 10^{-5} and δGDR=34\mbox{$\delta_{\rm GDR}$}=34. While the data are consistent with both of these possibilities, or any other combination of the above ratios, we must caution that the low values of αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} often recovered from CO-only methods (and after modeling only a few low-J CO lines) may be an artifact of well-known gas-dynamics effects, which are expected to have very little impact on the global C i line emission and none whatsoever on the corresponding dust continuum.

For galaxies at log LIR<11L_{\rm IR}<11 we can only use the ad sample (CO and dust continuum) because of the uncertainties surrounding the C icor galaxies. For the 88 galaxies at log LIR<11L_{\rm IR}<11 with CO and dust measurements, αCO=4.8−1.1+1.4\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}=4.8^{+1.4}_{-1.1} (including He), with ⟨κH⟩=1718\langle\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}\rangle=1718 kg m-2(δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}=122) but note that this is still a sample of massive and metal-rich galaxies, just at lower log LIR∼9−11L_{\rm IR}\sim 9-11. This study is not applicable to low mass metal-poor galaxies.

7 Conclusions

We have cross-calibrated the three mainstays of molecular gas measurements in extra-galactic astronomy: 12CO(1–0), [C i](P13{}^{3}P_{1}–P03{}^{3}P_{0}) and submm continuum emission from dust. This analysis uses galaxy samples spanning 0<z<50<z<5 and more than four orders of magnitude in LIRL_{\rm IR}. All the galaxies are metal rich and/or massive, to remove the need for large corrections for metallicity effects.

  • •

    We present a new method of optimising gas mass estimation when multiple tracers are observed, making use of the intrinsic scatter in all three pairs of gas tracers. We demonstrate its effectiveness compared to the simpler method used previously in the literature, and give examples and prescriptions for its use.

  • •

    In a purely empirical analysis, we show that LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} is the molecular gas tracer with the least intrinsic scatter, particularly at log LIR>11L_{\rm IR}>11. In such galaxies, LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} should be the preferred tracer, all other considerations being equal.

  • •

    Using our optimised method, we determine the mean empirical conversion factors for MmolM_{\rm mol} (including He). For log LIR>11L_{\rm IR}>11 these are: αC​IR=17.0±0.3{\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm C\,I}$}^{\rm R}=17.0\pm 0.3}, α850R=(6.9±0.1)×1012\mbox{$\alpha_{850}$}^{\rm R}=(6.9\pm 0.1)\times 10^{12}, αCOR=4.0±0.1\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}^{\rm R}=4.0\pm 0.1, with a scatter of 0.11-0.15 dex. These values are for an overall normalisation set to the average dust properties of local galaxies and diffuse dust in the Milky Way (κH\kappa_{\rm H}= δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}/ κ850\kappa_{850}= 1884 kg m−2\rm m^{-2}). A change in this choice of normalisation will affect αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} and αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} in a proportional manner and α850\alpha_{850} in an inversely proportional way. Our reference conversion values can be applied to any metal-rich galaxy with Z>0.5​Z⊙Z>0.5\,Z_{\odot} in the range 0<z<60<z<6.

  • •

    Using the same method we determine the principal mean physical parameters on which these conversion values depend. For galaxies at log LIR>11L_{\rm IR}>11: XC​IR=1.6×10−5{\mbox{$X_{\rm C\,I}$}^{\rm R}=1.6\times 10^{-5}}, κHR=1990​(δGDRR=141)\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}^{\rm R}=1990\,(\mbox{$\delta_{\rm GDR}$}^{\rm R}=141).

  • •

    The relationships between the observables, L850L_{850}, LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} and LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} are consistent with being linear and the ratios of these observables do not show a strong dependence on IR luminosity, dust temperature, redshift or the intensity of star formation.

  • •

    The ratio of LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} is marginally (3σ\sigma) different for MS galaxies and SMGs, with the latter having higher LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}, broadly consistent with expectations from astro-chemical cloud models that include enhanced cosmic rays.

  • •

    We find Q10=0.48\mbox{$Q_{10}$}=0.48 to be a reasonable choice for the excitation function (required to convert LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} to MC​IM_{\rm C\,I}), based on recent analysis showing that Q10Q_{10} has a super-thermal behaviour in non-LTE conditions (Papadopoulos et al., 2022). For a range of plausible galaxy ISM density and gas temperatures, the 99th percentile confidence interval on this value is ±16\pm 16 per cent.

  • •

    We present empirical relations for the mass-weighted dust temperature, TmwT_{\rm mw}, to allow observers to better estimate their dust calibration factors. We find a significant trend, where TmwT_{\rm mw} increases with LIRL_{\rm IR}. The median TmwT_{\rm mw} for SMGs at z∼2.5z\sim 2.5 is TmwSMG=30.1±0.7\mbox{$T_{\rm mw}$}^{\rm SMG}=30.1\pm 0.7 k, while for MS galaxies TmwMS=23.0±0.4\mbox{$T_{\rm mw}$}^{\rm\rm MS}=23.0\pm 0.4 k.

  • •

    We find a weak trend for κH\kappa_{\rm H} and XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} to increase with LIRL_{\rm IR}, and a similar trend for αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} to decrease. The empirical conversion factors (αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}, αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} and α850\alpha_{850}) also show a shallow but significant correlation with their tracer luminosities. These trends are not apparent if a constant TmwT_{\rm mw} is adopted. They are therefore driven by the change in TmwT_{\rm mw} with luminosity.

  • •

    Using an Occam’s Razor assumption that metal-rich galaxies have similar dust emissivity per unit gas mass, we find no evidence for the factor 3–4 αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} bi-modality between SMGs and MS galaxies often adopted in the literature. The shallow trends we do find reflect the common assumption that extreme SF systems have lower αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} and higher XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}, albeit at a far more subtle level, with only a ∼15\sim 15 per cent difference in the sample mean α850\alpha_{850} (higher), αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} (lower) and αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} (lower) for extreme star-forming galaxies versus ‘normal’ MS star-formers. o overall

  • •

    With the Occam’s Razor assumption, we also find no evidence to support the extremely high global estimates of XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} (∼6×10−5\sim 6\times 10^{-5}) reported in some literature for ULIRGs/SMGs – the high reported values are a consequence of assuming a low αCO∼1\mbox{$\alpha_{\rm CO}$}\sim 1. High XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} values may be expected, and indeed have been measured in small (<500<500pc) regions such as M82 (nuclear starbursts) and XDR regions around AGN, but the extent to which a global estimate would be enhanced depends on the dominance of that extreme environment in the galaxy’s H2 reservoir.

  • •

    One can, however, still postulate a different prior for the normalisation assumption and impose the popular bimodality in αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}. The constancy of the measured tracer luminosity ratios then forces the conversion factors for the other two tracers (dust and C i) to become bi-modal in the same way.

We conclude by noting that lacking a direct MH2M_{\rm H2} measurement method (i.e. via the H2\rm H_{2} lines themselves), one must assume a normalisation for one of the sample mean conversion factors in statistical studies like ours. In the present study we choose to benchmark to the dust emission, with κHN=1884\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}^{\rm N}=1884 kg m-2. Other normalisation choices can of course be made, but currently dust emission is the simplest and best understood tracer, and has the advantage of being totally insensitive to the gas-dynamic effects that affect the αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} conversion factor (e.g. unbound molecular gas components in the winds that exist in actively star-forming galaxies; winds which can be CO-bright while carrying little mass). The [C i](1–0) line emission will also be largely unaffected by these gas-dynamics effects, and as such the corresponding conversion factor, αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I}, shows promise as a good benchmark, borne out by the empirical finding that it has the least intrinsic scatter of the three tracers. With more extensive observational and theoretical studies of C i line emission (particularly in galaxies of lower IR luminosity), the limits of its usefulness as a gas tracer can be determined.

Appendix A Notes on the literature fluxes

In order to produce a homogeneous and up-to-date set of fluxes, we have applied the following corrections.

Corrections to previously published work:
  1. 1.

    Since Sco16 was published, the 500-μ\mum flux densities used for their local sample (Dale et al., 2012) were updated following the latest Herschel calibration. To estimate TmwT_{\rm mw}, TdT_{\rm d} and L850L_{850} we fitted the photometry presented by Chu et al. (2017) and Clark et al. (2018) using the method described in Dunne & Eales (2001).

  2. 2.

    The 850-μ\mum photometry for local galaxies in the SLUGS sample (Dunne et al., 2000) is contaminated by the CO(3–2) line. We have corrected for this using the results of Seaquist et al. (2004), where for galaxies with D<148D<148 Mpc we reduce the 850 μ\mum flux density by 25 per cent.

  3. 3.

    It appears that the CO(2–1) data from Aravena et al. (2016), as reproduced in Bothwell et al. (2017), has been incorrectly converted to L10′L^{\prime}_{10} (L21′L^{\prime}_{21} appears to have been multiplied by 0.9 instead of being divided by it). We have corrected this error and applied our chosen value of r21=0.8r_{21}=0.8 for the conversion.

Homogenisation of distances:

The most local galaxies (D<30D<30 Mpc) often have a variety of distances used in the literature. As we have often taken LIRL_{\rm IR}, LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}, LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} and L850L_{850} from different papers, we have had to homogenise the literature luminosities to correspond to a common distance. The distance chosen is that listed in Dale et al. (2017) and presented in Table 1.

Updating local CO data:

The Sco16 local galaxy sample used CO(1–0) fluxes from the FCRAO single-dish survey of Young et al. (1995), which has significant and uncertain extrapolations to total fluxes for extended galaxies. We have updated the CO data for these very local galaxies to use CO(1–0) maps from the COMING survey (Sorai et al., 2019) where possible as well as from other mapping datasets from the literature (Gao & Solomon, 2004; Kuno et al., 2007; Young et al., 2008; Galametz et al., 2011; Koda et al., 2011; Schruba et al., 2012; Ueda et al., 2014).

New CO measurement for ID141:

We use an unpublished CO(1–0) flux for ID141, which was observed with the Jansky Very Large Array and has S10=0.61±0.09​Jy​km s-1{S_{10}=0.61\pm 0.09\,\rm Jy\,\mbox{km\,s${}^{-1}$}}.

Appendix B Required corrections

B.1 H i-dominated galaxies at lower LIRL_{\rm IR}

There is a potential source of bias when deriving calibration factors involving L850L_{850} for galaxies with large ratios of fH​I=H i/H2\mbox{$f_{\rm H\,I}$}=\mbox{H\,{\sc i}}/\mbox{H${}_{2}$}, as the dust may be tracing H i as well as H2. If we apply our method from §3 to such H i-dominated galaxies, we will infer the presence of more H2 due to the dust which resides only in the H i phase. Because we calibrate in pairs of tracers, this leads to an over-estimate of αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} or αC​I\alpha_{\rm C\,I} as well as a bias in the dust-based calibration factor.

To investigate this, we estimated fH​If_{\rm H\,I} in the same regions as the submm flux densities for the local galaxies we could find in the literature (Dunne et al., 2000; Spekkens et al., 2004; Wong et al., 2013; Groves et al., 2015; Thuan et al., 2016; Dale et al., 2017; Koribalski et al., 2018; Jiao et al., 2021). As fH​If_{\rm H\,I} correlates inversely with M∗M_{\ast}, metallicity and LIRL_{\rm IR} (Bothwell et al., 2014; Saintonge et al., 2016, e.g.), this issue affects more of the low LIRL_{\rm IR} galaxies (mostly in the ad sample). For any galaxies with fH​I>1\mbox{$f_{\rm H\,I}$}>1 within the optical disk, we make a correction to L850L_{850}, removing that portion of the dust emission which is likely associated with the excess H i. This correction is designed to produce the same L850L_{850}/H2 ratio as a galaxy with fH​I=1\mbox{$f_{\rm H\,I}$}=1.

L850cor=L850​(2fH​I+1)\mbox{$L_{850}$}^{\rm cor}=\mbox{$L_{850}$}\left(\frac{2}{\mbox{$f_{\rm H\,I}$}+1}\right) (22)

Galaxies with fH​I>1\mbox{$f_{\rm H\,I}$}>1 are shown with this correction applied as cyan diamonds in the figures. The higher luminosity (U)LIRGs and SMGs are dominated by molecular gas (Yao et al., 2003, e.g.) so we do not need to correct these.

B.2 Discussion of local C i data

For the Herschel FTS measurements of local (U)LIRGs (Lu et al., 2017), we only include local galaxies with D>27D>27 Mpc to avoid issues with mis-matched beams. We also rejected galaxies where there was a large discrepancy between the measurement of Lu et al. (2017) and that of Kamenetzky et al. (2016) (using the same data).

The set of local galaxies which were mapped by the Herschel FTS and presented by J19 are shown in the figures, but not included in the averages for the following reasons:

  1. 1.

    The C i and CO measurements are made in matched apertures, however the area mapped in C i is sometimes much smaller than that used for the 500–850 μ\mum flux densities reported in the literature. Any analysis which involves both LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} and L850L_{850} requires a correction to LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} to address the mis-match in apertures. We attempted to do this by taking the global CO luminosities (which are equivalent global fluxes to the submm continuum measurements) and assume that the deficit between the global LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} and that measured in the same aperture as the C i by J19 is the same as the deficit in LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}:

    L′C​Icor=L′C​IJ19​LCO′globalLCO′J19\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}$}^{\rm cor}=\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}$}^{\rm J19}\frac{\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$}^{\rm global}}{\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}$}^{\rm J19}} (23)

    These corrections (JC) range from JC=0.00\rm JC=0.00–0.74 dex, and the pink diamonds in the figures indicate those galaxies that have JC>0.07\rm JC>0.07 dex. Even after applying the corrections, the J19 galaxies have different average properties in the L850L_{850}/LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} ratio (see Fig. 2). We therefore, do not have confidence in our comparison of LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} to L850L_{850} for these galaxies and so exclude them from the statistics.

  2. 2.

    Although the CO and C i luminosities from J19 are measured in the same apertures, there is a trend for these resolved galaxies to have lower LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} for a given LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} compared to galaxies which have more global flux measurements. There could be a sampling bias because C i is only detected over the inner kpc or so of the larger galaxies. The CO luminosity per mass of gas (αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}) has been found to be lower in the central regions of many galaxies (Sandstrom et al., 2013), which would produce a decrease in LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}. Since we wish to compare the same averaged global fluxes across all galaxies, we remove these ‘centrally-biased’ galaxies from our statistical analysis, but we show them in the figures for completeness.

  3. 3.

    Finally, a more recent paper by Jiao et al. (2021) did produce matched dust and C i measurements for a subset of the J19 galaxies. The results are shown in Fig. 3(d) where it can be seen that the J21 galaxies are still deficient in C i compared to the higher luminosity galaxies. This cannot be due to a mis-matched aperture but the same sampling bias is present toward the inner regions of the resolved galaxies. An offset to lower LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} per L850L_{850} implies either depressed LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} (lower XC​IX_{\rm C\,I}) or increased L850L_{850} per unit gas mass (lower δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}, or higher dust emissivity).

  4. 4.

    Unfortunately, this is the only published set of C i fluxes for galaxies with log⁡LC​I′<8\log\mbox{$L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}$}<8 and the only set of fluxes published for the mapping mode of the Herschel FTS. There is no description in the literature of how the processing for this mode should be made, and there are differences in the results of J19 and Crocker et al. (2019), who analyse some of the same mapping data. Despite our best attempts to contact the relevant team, we have not been given the details of their flux measurements. We can only note that the C i fluxes from Herschel FTS mapping are not necessarily repeatable when analysed by different teams and so elect to exclude the resolved J19 galaxies from the statistical analysis.

Excluded galaxies are denoted as ‘C icor’ and they are shown as pink diamonds on the relevant figures.

Appendix C Dust mass opacity and the relationship of dust to gas

The dust mass opacity coefficient, κd​(λ)\kappa_{\rm d}(\lambda), is proportional to the emissivity per unit mass of dust. It is related to the calibration parameter we use in our analysis, κH=δGDR/κd\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}=\mbox{$\delta_{\rm GDR}$}/\kappa_{\rm d}, where κH\kappa_{\rm H} refers to the dust emission per H mass, thus encompassing the two unknowns of dust optical properties and gas-to-dust ratio (δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}).

The dust optical properties are not easily measured, and can vary enormously from laboratory-based studies to theoretical dust models and from those inferred by observations (for a review see Dunne et al., 2003; Clark et al., 2019b, e.g).

Commonly adopted extragalactic estimates range from κ850=0.03\kappa_{850}=0.03–0.08​m2​kg−10.08\,\rm m^{2}\,kg^{-1} (Li & Draine, 2001; Dunne et al., 2000; James et al., 2002; Draine, 2003; Planck Collaboration XIX, 2011; Eales et al., 2012; Clark et al., 2016; Bianchi et al., 2019), though higher values (by factors of several) are inferred for the very densest and coldest environments where grains can grow icy mantles and coagulate (Köhler et al., 2015; Remy et al., 2017; Ysard et al., 2018). These changes in opacity have also been correlated with a loss of PAH and stochastically heated small grains (Flagey et al., 2009; Ysard et al., 2013). Remy et al. (2017) suggest that regions of the ISM with dust opacities a factor ∼2\sim 2 higher than the diffuse ISM (and with cold dust, Td∼16\mbox{$T_{\rm d}$}\sim 16–18 k), would be those where grains are accreting carbonaceous mantles, as in the THEMIS dust model (Jones et al., 2017; Jones, 2018). This carbon mantle-accreting regime is largely assumed to be the dark neutral medium (close to the atomic-molecular transition, where there is low CO emission and high H i opacity). Deeper within clouds, where the temperature drops to Td<16\mbox{$T_{\rm d}$}<16 k, the dust begins to aggregate and accrete ice mantles, which increases the opacity further. These very dense, cold environments do not, however, contain the bulk of the ISM mass and certainly do not emit a dominant fraction of L850L_{850} in a galaxy (Draine et al., 2007; Bianchi et al., 2019). The increase in dust emissivity (κ850\kappa_{850}) from atomic to moderately dense molecular material is in the range 1.2–2.0 (Remy et al., 2017).

In fact, it is κH\kappa_{\rm H} – the parameter relating the dust emissivity to the gas mass – that can be measured in astrophysical situations, since we have no absolute knowledge of δGDR\delta_{\rm GDR}. Table 15 lists a comprehensive set of observational and theoretical values for κH\kappa_{\rm H} from the literature. Estimates of κH\kappa_{\rm H} in the Milky Way are made across a number of sight-lines, from H i-only (diffuse) to H2-dominated clouds (dense) where CO emission is used with assumptions about αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} in order to determine NHN_{\rm H}. Independent confirmation is provided by studies (Remy et al., 2017, e.g.) using γ\gamma-ray observations to determine the gas column; the resulting values of κH\kappa_{\rm H} are in good agreement (see Table 15), with κH\kappa_{\rm H} being higher along diffuse sight-lines (1800–2400), dropping to 700–1500 in denser molecular or dark neutral media.

In extragalactic studies, a similar method is used, although with larger uncertainties as it is less straightforward to decompose the atomic and molecular components along the line of sight. These studies find a range of κH=1500\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}=1500–2200 kg m-2, closer to the diffuse ISM measurements in the Milky Way.

For a given dust model, we can also calculate the theoretical κH\kappa_{\rm H} given the assumed dust optical properties, chemical abundances and depletions. The theoretical values are also listed in Table 15 where the current consensus is for κH∼1900\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}\sim 1900–2000 kg m-2. The popular Draine (2003) model has a significantly higher κH=3200\mbox{$\kappa_{\rm H}$}=3200 kg m-2 (lower κ850=0.034\mbox{$\kappa_{850}$}=0.034 m2 kg-1 for δGDR=109\mbox{$\delta_{\rm GDR}$}=109) than all of the empirical measurements. This was noted by Draine et al. (2014) and Planck Collaboration XXIX (2016) and has been updated in the more recent version of this model by Hensley & Draine (2021). We encourage readers to use the updated version in order to produce dust-based measurements which are consistent with what we know about dust from observations.

Appendix D Deriving gas mass from observations of [C i](P13{}^{3}P_{1}–P03{}^{3}P_{0})

The excitation term, QulQ_{\rm ul}, which describes the fraction of C atoms in each excited state, is a function of (nn,TkT_{\rm k}) in non-LTE conditions, and is derived analytically in the Appendix to Papadopoulos et al. (2004). A recent study of the [C i](2–1)/(1–0) line ratio found that [C i](2–1) is strongly sub-thermally excited, and [C i](1–0) presents interesting super-thermal behaviour in the range of density and temperature expected for galaxies. We illustrate the dependence of QulQ_{\rm ul} on (nn,TkT_{\rm k}) in Fig. 13. As discussed by Papadopoulos et al. (2022), the value of Q10Q_{10} for lower densities (n=300n=300–3000 cm-3) can exceed the LTE value at TkT_{\rm k}>20 k, but Fig. 13 shows that for a reasonable range of nn and TkT_{\rm k} (300<n<10,000300<n<10,000 cm-3, 25<Tk<8025<\mbox{$T_{\rm k}$}<80 k) Q10Q_{10} does not go outside the range 0.35–0.53. In fact, for a uniform probability of (2.4<log⁡n<4.02.4<\log n<4.0) and (25<Tk<8025<\mbox{$T_{\rm k}$}<80 k) the 99 per cent range for Q10Q_{10} is 0.40–0.54, median=0.48. The relative uncertainty on the calibration of C i mass from the lack of knowledge of (nn,TkT_{\rm k}) is thus <±16<\pm 16 per cent. We will therefore use the median value of Q10=0.48\mbox{$Q_{10}$}=0.48 throughout, because even though we may be able to use the measured TdT_{\rm d} to infer the galaxies with higher or lower TkT_{\rm k} (assuming Tk=αTD​Td\mbox{$T_{\rm k}$}=\alpha^{\rm TD}\,\mbox{$T_{\rm d}$} – see Papadopoulos et al., 2022), the lack of knowledge of the density and the super-thermal behaviour in the J=1J=1 state means that there is no direct correlation between Q10Q_{10} and TkT_{\rm k}. Using sensible average parameters for MS galaxies [and SMGs], so nn=500 [5,000] cm-3and TkT_{\rm k} = 40 [80] K we find only a small (∼\sim 10  per cent) difference in the Q10Q_{10} values expected.

The LTE expressions for Q10Q_{10} and TxT_{\rm x} should not be used (Papadopoulos et al., 2022) as Q10LTE\rm Q_{10}^{LTE} is actually lower than the non-LTE Q10Q_{10} for densities higher than a few hundred cm-3, and thus its use would lead to a systematic bias - e.g. for TkT_{\rm k}=60 K and n=1000cm-3, the LTE value for Q10Q_{10} is 18  per cent lower than the appropriate non-LTE value. This would lead to an 18  per cent over-estimate of the H2 mass using C i.

For the [C i](2–1) line, things are not so promising (Fig. 13(right)). The range of possible values of Q21Q_{21} are large, ranging from 0.07–0.37 for the 99 per cent range. The median is Q21=0.22Q_{21}=0.22, giving an uncertainty range of ±68\pm 68 per cent for reasonable values of (nn,TkT_{\rm k}). Because of the sub-thermal behaviour, the [C i](2–1) line is a sensitive indicator of density (Papadopoulos et al., 2022) and galaxies with strong [C i](2–1) emission will have a larger fraction of their H2 in a dense state.

Appendix E From pairwise variances to individual variances

We have measurements of different tracers of gas mass for several galaxies, but no direct measurements of MH2M_{\rm H2} itself. Hence, it is not possible to measure directly how well each tracer follows the gas mass. However, we do have measurements of the different tracers for each galaxy, so we can estimate the scatter in the difference between the tracers. Under some assumptions this allows us to infer the scatter between each tracer and the gas mass.

To simplify the notation, we write the log of observed quantities and corresponding standard deviation of errors as

x1\displaystyle x_{1} =log⁡(L850),\displaystyle=\rm\log(L_{850}), σ1=log⁡(1+σ850/L850),\displaystyle\sigma_{1}=\rm\log(1+\sigma_{850}/L_{850}), (24)
x2\displaystyle x_{2} =log⁡(LCO′),\displaystyle=\rm\log(L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}), σ2=log⁡(1+σCO/LCO′),\displaystyle\sigma_{2}=\rm\log(1+\sigma_{\rm CO}/L^{\prime}_{CO}),
x3\displaystyle x_{3} =log⁡(LC​I′),\displaystyle=\rm\log(L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}), σ3=log⁡(1+σC​I/LC​I′).\displaystyle\sigma_{3}=\rm\log(1+\sigma_{\rm C\,I}/L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}).

If true value of the log of the gas mass is m^=log⁡(MH2)\hat{m}=\log(\mbox{$M_{\rm H2}$}), and the true values of the observed quantities are x^i\hat{x}_{i}, where i=1​…​3i=1...3, then we can write

m^=x^i+a^i,\hat{m}=\hat{x}_{i}+\hat{a}_{i}, (25)

where a^i\hat{a}_{i} are the true calibration factors for each galaxy,

a^1=\displaystyle\hat{a}_{1}= −log⁡(α^850)\displaystyle-\rm\log(\hat{\alpha}_{850}) (26)
a^2=\displaystyle\hat{a}_{2}= log⁡(α^CO)\displaystyle\rm\displaystyle\log(\hat{\alpha}_{CO})
a^3=\displaystyle\hat{a}_{3}= log⁡(α^C​I)\displaystyle\rm\displaystyle\log(\hat{\alpha}_{C\,I})

Note that the true values a^i\hat{a}_{i} may be different for each galaxy, depending on the individual physical conditions within the galaxies.

If we choose a particular set calibration factors for all galaxies, say a~i\tilde{a}_{i}, this provides three estimates of the gas mass for each galaxy,

mi=xi+a~im_{i}=x_{i}+\tilde{a}_{i} (27)

The error in each mass estimate is

mi−m^\displaystyle m_{i}-\hat{m} =xi−xi^+a~i−a^i\displaystyle=x_{i}-\hat{x_{i}}+\tilde{a}_{i}-\hat{a}_{i} (28)
=δ​xi+δ​ai\displaystyle=\delta x_{i}+\delta a_{i}

where δ​ai\delta a_{i} is the difference between the true factor for this galaxy and the value we have chosen, and δ​xi\delta x_{i} are the measurement errors of the observations. If we assume that the errors on xix_{i} are not correlated with the errors on aia_{i}, then the variance of the mass errors is given by:

var⁡(mi−m^)=σi2+si2\mathrm{var}(m_{i}-\hat{m})=\sigma_{i}^{2}+s_{i}^{2} (29)

where si2s_{i}^{2} is the variance of the true calibration factors.

The value of si2s_{i}^{2} gives a direct measure of how accurate the particular tracer is when using a universal calibration factor for all galaxies. Without knowing the true gas mass, we do not have a direct measure of this value, but we can obtain an estimate by considering the differences between the mass measurements:

mi−mj\displaystyle m_{i}-m_{j} =xi−xj+a~i−a~j\displaystyle=x_{i}-x_{j}+\tilde{a}_{i}-\tilde{a}_{j} (30)
=δ​xi−δ​xj+δ​ai−δ​aj\displaystyle=\delta x_{i}-\delta x_{j}+\delta a_{i}-\delta a_{j}

If we ignore all co-variance terms, the variance of the differences is given by:

vi​j=var⁡(mi−mj)=σi2+σj2+si2+sj2v_{ij}=\mathrm{var}(m_{i}-m_{j})=\sigma_{i}^{2}+\sigma_{j}^{2}+s_{i}^{2}+s_{j}^{2} (31)

It is straightforward to re-arrange these equations to find the intrinsic variance of the calibration factors as:

s02=(v01−v12+v20)/2−σ02s_{0}^{2}=\left(v_{01}-v_{12}+v_{20}\right)/2-\sigma_{0}^{2} (32)

with similar equations for s12s_{1}^{2}, and s22s_{2}^{2}. So long as we have good estimates of the measurement errors, σi\sigma_{i}, for the observed quantities, we can estimate the scatter in calibration constants for each tracer. Using our dataset we have measured the variance for each pair of factors in Eqn. 31. Assuming that the co-variance between the calibration factors is zero, we use the three pair variances to estimate the intrinsic variance of the three individual calibration factors. The resulting standard deviations are sκ=0.1294s_{\kappa}=0.1294, sα=0.1436s_{\alpha}=0.1436 and sX=0.1125s_{\mathrm{X}}=0.1125, using all galaxies except the C icor3737 37 When restricting the analysis to log LIR>11L_{\rm IR}>11 galaxies, C i produces notably less scatter than both CO and dust continuum, with sκ=0.1339s_{\kappa}=0.1339, sα=0.1646s_{\alpha}=0.1646 and sX=0.082s_{\mathrm{X}}=0.082.. Values are listed in Table 3.

This analysis shows that XC​IX_{\rm C\,I} has the smallest scatter between galaxies, especially when considering log LIR>11L_{\rm IR}>11 galaxies, which is a new result, independent of any assumptions.

Appendix F A Bayesian approach to combining gas mass estimates

Our method of combining the three gas mass tracers is based on the idea that the conversion factors for any particular galaxy come from parent distributions with variances as derived in Appendix E. This means that we should allow for the expected scatter in conversion factors as well as the observational error when combining estimates from the different tracers. Using a Bayesian approach to the problem, we show the most likely mass estimate is simply the inverse variance weighted mean of the tracers, where the weights include both measurement error and the variance in conversion factors.

We continue to use the the notation as in Appendix E, where the observed quantities are xix_{i} and errors σi\sigma_{i}. Assuming the measurement errors are Gaussian the probability of measuring the observed value of xix_{i} is

P⁡(xi|x^i,σi)=𝒩⁡(xi|x^i,σi2)P(x_{i}|\hat{x}_{i},\sigma_{i})={\cal N}(x_{i}|\hat{x}_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2}) (33)

where 𝒩\cal N represents the normal distribution centred on x^i\hat{x}_{i} and with variance σi2\sigma_{i}^{2}. Now, for each observation we can use Bayes theorem to estimate the posterior probability that the gas mass is mm,

P⁡(m,a^i|xi)=P⁡(xi|m,a^i)​P​(a^i)​P​(m)/P⁡(xi)P(m,\hat{a}_{i}|x_{i})=P(x_{i}|m,\hat{a}_{i})P(\hat{a}_{i})P(m)/P(x_{i}) (34)

where we have assumed mm and a^i\hat{a}_{i} are independent. For the prior on a^i\hat{a}_{i}, we assume a normal distribution with mean a¯i\bar{a}_{i} and variance si2s_{i}^{2}, as discussed in Appendix E . We assume a flat prior on mm, implying that P⁡(m)P(m) is constant. Since P⁡(xi)P(x_{i}) is also constant, the position of the maximum posterior probability does not depend on the actual value of P⁡(m)/P⁡(xi)P(m)/P(x_{i}), and for convenience we set this to 1. Therefore:

P⁡(m,a^i|xi)∝P⁡(xi|m,a^i)​P​(a^i)=𝒩⁡(xi|m−a^i,σi2)​𝒩​(a^i|a¯i,si2)=𝒩⁡(a^i|m−xi,σi2)​𝒩​(a^i|a¯i,si2).\begin{split}P(m,\hat{a}_{i}|x_{i})&\propto P(x_{i}|m,\hat{a}_{i})P(\hat{a}_{i})\\ &={\cal N}(x_{i}|m-\hat{a}_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2}){\cal N}(\hat{a}_{i}|\bar{a}_{i},s_{i}^{2})\\ &={\cal N}(\hat{a}_{i}|m-x_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2}){\cal N}(\hat{a}_{i}|\bar{a}_{i},s_{i}^{2}).\end{split} (35)

Here we have used Equation 25 to go from m−a^im-\hat{a}_{i} to m−xim-x_{i}. Since we are interested primarily in the value of the gas mass, and not explicitly in the values of the calibration factors, we can marginalise over the values of a^i\hat{a}_{i}. Ignoring the uncertainties on the variances, σi2\sigma_{i}^{2} and si2s_{i}^{2}, leads to:

P⁡(m|xi)=𝒩⁡(m|xi+a¯i,σi2+si2).P(m|x_{i})={\cal N}(m|x_{i}+\bar{a}_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2}+s_{i}^{2}). (36)

Including all three observations for the galaxy this becomes

P⁡(m|{xi})=∏i=13𝒩⁡(m|xi+a¯i,σi2+si2)∝exp(−∑i=13(m−xi−a¯i)22​(σi2+si2)).\begin{split}P(m|\{x_{i}\})&=\prod_{i=1}^{3}{\cal N}(m|x_{i}+\bar{a}_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2}+s_{i}^{2})\\ &\propto\exp\left(-\sum_{i=1}^{3}\frac{(m-x_{i}-\bar{a}_{i})^{2}}{2(\sigma_{i}^{2}+s_{i}^{2})}\right).\end{split} (37)

So maximising the posterior probability with respect to mm is equivalent to minimising χ2\chi^{2}, where:

χ2=∑i=13(m−xi−a¯i)22​(σi2+si2).\chi^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\frac{(m-x_{i}-\bar{a}_{i})^{2}}{2(\sigma_{i}^{2}+s_{i}^{2})}. (38)

The minimum with respect to mm is given by

mopt=(∑i=13xi+ai¯σi2+si2)/(∑i=131σi2+si2)=(∑i=13(xi+ai¯)​wi)/(∑i=13wi),\begin{split}m^{\rm opt}&=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{3}\frac{x_{i}+\bar{a_{i}}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}+s_{i}^{2}}\right)\Bigg/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{3}\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}^{2}+s_{i}^{2}}\right)\\ &=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{3}(x_{i}+\bar{a_{i}})w_{i}\right)\Bigg/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{3}w_{i}\right),\end{split} (39)

where wi=1/(σi2+si2)w_{i}=1/(\sigma_{i}^{2}+s_{i}^{2}). So the optimal mass estimate is simply the inverse variance-weighted mean of the three estimates, where each uses the mean conversion factor, and where the variance for each measure is the sum of the measurement error and the expected variance of the conversion factor.

The uncertainty on moptm^{\rm opt} is the uncertainty on the weighted mean,

σmopt=1/(∑i=13wi).\sigma_{m^{\rm opt}}=1\Bigg/\left(\sum_{i=1}^{3}w_{i}\right). (40)

The corresponding estimates of the conversion factors for a particular galaxy are then simply given by:

ai=m−xi,i=1​…​3a_{i}=m-x_{i},\quad i=1...3 (41)

The uncertainty on the factor aia_{i} depends on the uncertainty on moptm^{\rm opt}, from equation 40, and the uncertainty on the measurement xix_{i}, from equation 24. Since the estimate of mm depends on the measurements xix_{i}, there is a non-zero covariance between mm and xix_{i}. Allowing for this covariance, the expected uncertainty on aia_{i} is given by:

σai2=σmopt2+σi2​(1−2​wi∑i=13wi).\sigma_{a_{i}}^{2}=\sigma_{\rm m^{opt}}^{2}+\sigma_{i}^{2}\left(1-\frac{2w_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{3}w_{i}}\right). (42)

Appendix G Sensitivity of tracer to SFR and radiation field intensity

Fig. 14 shows the observable ratios, L850L_{850}/LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} and L850L_{850}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO}, as a function of TdT_{\rm d} (left) and LIRL_{\rm IR} (right). There is no significant trend for L850L_{850}/LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} or L850L_{850}/LCO′L^{\prime}_{\rm CO} with either TdT_{\rm d} or LIRL_{\rm IR}. There is a noticeable offset to higher L850L_{850}/LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}for the C icor galaxies (pink diamonds), which also have lower TdT_{\rm d} and LIRL_{\rm IR} than the other samples. As these galaxies require large corrections to LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I} in order to compare to L850L_{850}, we cannot be sure if this is a real effect, or just an under-estimate of the required correction. A larger sample of low-temperature, low-luminosity galaxies with matched apertures will be required to investigate this.

Appendix H Tests of robustness

H.1 Consistency of parameter estimates

We investigated the consistency of our parameter estimates for the same galaxies when three tracers are used compared to only two. Fig. 15 shows that there is a reasonable correlation between the three-tracer and two-tracer estimates, with only small differences in the sample medians when different numbers of tracers are used. The Xd pair produces the closest match to the method with three pairs (Fig. 15 centre and lower-right panels), with no bias and a small scatter. If restricted to choosing only one pair to observe, the best choice seems to be L850L_{850} and LC​I′L^{\prime}_{\rm C\,I}.

H.2 Impact of using fixed vs. variable TmwT_{\rm mw}

In this section we test a different approach to TmwT_{\rm mw}, one of the main physical dependencies that impacts on the calibration of gas masses3838 38 This is not to suggest that αCO\alpha_{\rm CO} is not dependent on the physical properties of the gas, but being optically thick, this line does not have any simple relationship with anything we can empirically determine. Similarly, we have shown that Q10Q_{10} is not easy to determine per galaxy, but its range is small enough to have no significant impact on our calibration study.. To estimate gas mass from L850L_{850}, the mass-weighted dust temperature, TmwT_{\rm mw}, is required. TmwT_{\rm mw} has been set to 25 k in previous studies (Scoville et al., 2014; Scoville et al., 2016; Hughes et al., 2017, e.g.), adding to the uncertainty in gas-mass estimates for individual galaxies. However, as we wish to study trends in the conversion factors, we are concerned about the possible effects of systematic trends in TmwT_{\rm mw}, since these may affect the resulting behaviour of the conversion factors if ignored.

Having determined empirical relationships between zz, LIRL_{\rm IR}, SED colour (LIRL_{\rm IR}/L850L_{850}) and TmwT_{\rm mw} in §2.3.1, we compare the calibration results using these empirically determined TmwT_{\rm mw} to the standard assumption of constant TmwT_{\rm mw}=25 k made in the literature. Fig. 17 shows the impact of using our empirical relations (coloured points), versus keeping TmwT_{\rm mw} fixed (grey points). Each panel shows one of the affected conversion factors derived from either the ad or Xd samples. The trends with luminosity – visible for our default prescription – disappear when a constant Tmw=25\mbox{$T_{\rm mw}$}=25 k is used.

The histogram of the offsets in each conversion factor when using the empirical TmwT_{\rm mw} compared to constant Tmw=25\mbox{$T_{\rm mw}$}=25 k (Fig. 16) shows that the choice of TmwT_{\rm mw} makes no significant difference to the median values of the parameters (<0.015<0.015 dex). For individual galaxies, the average uncertainty introduced by using a constant TmwT_{\rm mw} is 0.046–0.06 dex (1σ\sigma), with a maximum of ∼0.2\sim 0.2 dex.

Finally, the difference in the gas-mass estimates, MH2M_{\rm H2}, when using constant TmwT_{\rm mw} versus our empirical prescription is shown in Fig. 18. At lower LIRL_{\rm IR}, a constant TmwT_{\rm mw} produces lower MH2M_{\rm H2} compared to our empirical method, because these galaxies are local disks which tend to have colder diffuse dust temperatures. At higher log LIRL_{\rm IR}>12>12, the trend reverses as the diffuse dust temperatures increase to ∼30\sim 30 k.

Appendix I A robust Orthogonal Distance Regression algorithm

In order to fit the most robust linear model to the data, we have employed an Orthogonal Distance Regression and included intrinsic scatter. 3939 39 These ideas are outlined in Hogg et al. (2010) and Foreman-Mackey (2017), however both of their Bayesian implementations result in biases in the estimate slope. The biases are quite pronounced when the range sampled by the data is not much larger than the errors on the data, but are significant even when the range sampled is ∼\sim10σ\sigma. The biases also depend on which axis is chosen as the “true” independent variable and whether the errors are asymmetrical (σx≪σy\sigma_{x}\ll\sigma_{y}, or σx≫σy\sigma_{x}\gg\sigma_{y}). We found that an ODR which does not use the Bayesian likelihood formalism is the only one which does not have such biases; hence our choice to use it here.

We use the emcee MCMC sampler (Foreman-Mackey et al., 2013) to explore the χ2\chi^{2} space and compute robust confidence intervals. Our algorithm results in parameters which are symmetric under transformation of xx and yy, allowing us to utilise the full co-variance matrix, including the intrinsic scatter as a third variable.

The MCMC is set up to explore the following likelihood function:

LnL=−0.5∑i=1N(Δ2/σ2+ln(σ2/S2))LnL=-0.5\sum^{N}_{i=1}(\Delta^{2}/\sigma^{2}+\ln(\sigma^{2}/S_{2})) (43)
Δ=𝐯.𝐙−b​cos⁡(θ)\Delta={\bf v.Z}-b\,\cos(\theta)

with 𝐙{\bf Z} as the data array of xx and yy values, bb as the intercept and θ\theta related to the slope as m=t​a​n​(θ)m=tan(\theta). vv is a matrix to rotate to find the perpendicular distances, given by 𝐯=[−s​i​n​(θ),c​o​s​(θ)]{\bf v}=[-sin(\theta),cos(\theta)].

σ2=(𝐒+𝚲m.𝐯).𝐯\sigma^{2}=({\bf S+\Lambda_{\rm m}.v}).{\bf v}

where 𝐒{\bf S} is the co-variance matrix. To include intrinsic scatter in the orthogonal direction, as well as measurement errors into the fitting, we add a term to the co-variance matrix, as suggested in Foreman-Mackey (2017):

𝚲m=(tan⁡(θ)2−tan⁡(θ)−tan⁡(θ)1.0)×cos⁡(θ)2×e2​ln⁡(λ){\bf\Lambda_{\rm m}}=\begin{pmatrix}\tan(\theta)^{2}&-\tan(\theta)\\ -\tan(\theta)&1.0\\ \end{pmatrix}\times\cos(\theta)^{2}\times e^{2\,\ln(\lambda)} (44)
S2=(𝐒.𝐯).𝐯S_{2}=({\bf S.v}).{\bf v}

The initial conditions were given by the ordinary least-squares fit parameters for variance in the yy direction. The run was checked to ensure adequate burn-in and independence between samples. We used 32 random walkers with 6,000 steps each.
